When PlayStation 3 became a military supercomputer?!👀

In 2010, the U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory built a supercomputer using an unusual piece of hardware: 1,760 Sony PlayStation 3 consoles.

The project, called Condor Cluster, was based in Rome, New York, and was used for tasks such as radar optimization, satellite image processing, and AI research. At the time, it ranked among the world’s most powerful supercomputers, reaching around 500 TFLOPS of computing performance.

The reason behind the unusual choice was simple: price and efficiency.

The PlayStation 3’s Cell processor and graphics hardware offered impressive parallel computing capabilities for a fraction of the cost of traditional supercomputer components. The entire system reportedly cost about $2 million - only a small percentage of what a comparable machine would have required using conventional hardware.

Another key factor was that the PS3 could run Linux, allowing researchers to use thousands of consoles as a massive computing cluster.

Condor Cluster became an early example of consumer hardware being repurposed for serious scientific and military workloads. Years later, GPUs would become the backbone of modern AI training, but this project showed the same idea ahead of its time: massive computing power can come from unexpected places.

The experiment did not last forever. After Sony removed Linux support from later PlayStation updates, building similar clusters became impractical. The successor, PlayStation 4, also lacked the same flexibility.

A gaming console designed for entertainment briefly became a weapon in the computing race - a reminder that the future of hardware is often hidden in places nobody expects.

$QS Q2'26 — deep dive.

① The PowerCo amendment isn't a downgrade, it's a change in nature.SOW-1 ran on cost-share: PowerCo reimbursed expenses incurred against an agreed scope. SOW-2 shifts to milestone-based: QS gets paid on delivery. The cap comes down, yes — but Hettrich confirms projected expenses come down in mirror, with a net neutral cash impact versus the 2025 scope. Part of the reduction simply comes from eliminating the MotoE milestones, the racing series being on hiatus. So we removed milestones that became moot, not milestones that were missed.
What actually changes: stronger incentive alignment, more schedule risk. If milestones slip, the cash slips with them.

② The royalty prepay is untouched — and its release condition is the real signal. UBS question, direct answer: the prepay is unchanged, released by technical milestones and form factor alignment. That last phrase points to a SOW-2 clause few people have opened: the "QSE5 Target Design," meaning the version PowerCo will choose to mass produce and into which QSE-5 technology gets incorporated. The choice belongs to PowerCo, not QS.

This converges naturally with the Einheitszelle VW has been pushing since Power Day: a standardized prismatic format meant to cover most of the group's lineup. If the Target Design is that unified cell, the nature of the deal changes — QS is no longer selling a cell, it's supplying a chemistry into a format VW has already standardized industrially across Salzgitter, Valencia, St. Thomas. Not confirmed by name. But the clause is written precisely to allow it.
③ Cobra at larger format: the real technical point of the quarter.QS demonstrated the process can produce larger-area separators for higher-capacity cell designs. Three readings that reinforce each other:

First, it confirms by implication that QSE-5 alone doesn't cover large-format auto + data center + defense. Multi-format becomes necessary, not optional.

Second, SOW-2 explicitly includes "larger format cells" milestones — so PowerCo is funding that evolution.
Third, and most importantly, Cobra has always been QS's historical bottleneck. The fact that it absorbs a surface-area increase without full re-tooling is structurally more significant than any customer announcement this quarter. It's also the brick that can unlock the form factor alignment from point ②.

④ The three verticals: a commercial architecture, not a rebrand.QSEV, QSDC, QSAS. Sivaram's logic is economic: auto customers all have their own pilot lines and mass production capability. Data center and defense customers don't. So different go-to-market, ODMs involved, and above all a product integration that offers "more opportunities for value creation."

Translation: on auto, QS licenses and collects a royalty. On DC and defense, QS could capture more value per cell for lack of a partner industrializing on its behalf. Potentially higher margin — but capex to carry itself.

The hiring confirms the intent: QSDC's GM comes from Broadcom, SanDisk, Micron, Marvell, MediaTek. Zero battery background, one hundred percent semiconductor and data center. You hire that profile to sell to data center architects, not to do cell R&D.

⑤ The defense shipment, and what Sivaram actually says about it.QSE-5 cells shipped to a "major American defense prime." Unnamed. Asked whether it was natural ramp or capacity freed by a deferral, he answers "the answer is yes," then specifies that Eagle Line's productivity gains "naturally" enabled the shipment.
So: it's a byproduct of pilot cadence, not a structured contract. Encouraging on execution, but not yet a design win.

On identity, two credible and purely speculative threads. Ross Niebergall has sat on the board since March: former President of Aerojet Rocketdyne, former CTO of L3Harris and Harris, former VP Engineering at Raytheon, former CEO of ThalesRaytheon. And Mark Maybury, former Chief Scientist of the US Air Force, now VP Commercialization at Lockheed Martin, sits on the strategic advisory board. Two real networks, zero confirmation.

The underlying argument is sturdier than the name: conventional Li-ion depends on graphite anode material sourced almost exclusively from China. The anode-free architecture eliminates that component entirely. For an American prime, that isn't a marginal advantage, it's an eligibility condition.

⑥ The unresolved contradiction: QSDC has a deadline, not a capacity.Sivaram is explicit on timing: the 800V DC transition and megawatt racks deploy in data centers toward end of 2028, so you have to be ready ahead of that. He calls them "natural deadlines" imposed by the market. The data center qualification cycle is structurally shorter than auto — QSDC could therefore generate revenue before the PowerCo SOP.
Except Hettrich drops the key admission of the call: Eagle Line is a powerful sampling capability, but "in the fullness of time, we absolutely will need to add capacity." Today, outside automotive, QS has a fraction of licensed capacity permitted via PowerCo since the 2025 amendment, and nothing else. And capex was revised downward this quarter.

Either capacity comes from a partner — consistent with the asset-light licensing model — or a raise is coming. That's the dilution risk the market hasn't priced yet.

⑦ Safety: the one area where QS can prove superiority today.IEC 62660-2 / SAE J2464 protocol. QSE-5 passes all three tests — thermal stability, external short circuit, nail penetration. No competing cell tested passes all three. And QS tests thermal stability well beyond the point where conventional Li-ion testing stops.

That's the differentiating argument for data center — sitting next to very high-value GPU racks — and for defense. And it's demonstrable now, without waiting for SOP.

⑧ Tim Holme on a temporary modified arrangement — the item nobody flagged.Not in the letter, not on the call. It's in the 10-Q, filed in lieu of an 8-K Item 5.02.
The facts: from August 2026 through May 2027, the cofounder and CTO moves to a "temporary modified work arrangement" to spend an extended period with his family. He remains an employee, remains CTO, and retains oversight of long-term R&D priorities. Certain day-to-day responsibilities get reassigned to long-tenured members of the senior technical team. On compensation: base salary paused, vesting of purely service-based RSUs paused, but other equity awards continue vesting under existing terms.

How I read it. The compensation structure is the best available tell, and it argues for the benign reading: an executive on the way out gets bought out, not put on salary pause. Suspending salary and time-based vesting while maintaining performance-linked awards is the design of a framed sabbatical, with an explicit return date and an R&D scope preserved. The "look forward to his return to full duties" language points the same direction.

The honest counterargument: a cofounder CTO stepping back for ten months a few quarters ahead of technology transfer to PowerCo, at a company whose entire thesis rests on technical execution, is never neutral. And context matters — he's been selling steadily under a 10b5-1 plan in recent months, which will mechanically feed the pessimistic reading even though those sales are pre-programmed and unrelated.

The real test will be the reassignment. QS refers to "long-tenured members of our senior technical team" without naming them. If the organization absorbs the temporary absence without drift on Eagle Line and on the larger-format milestones, it's a non-event and it demonstrates bench depth nobody was crediting. If milestones slip in H2, the reading changes retroactively. Worth watching, without over-reading it in either direction.
⑨ What I take away.The quarter is a story of commercial structuring, not industrialization. QS built the go-to-market architecture, secured a fourth Top-10 OEM with Honda, shipped cells to a fifth, proved Cobra scales in surface area, and published safety data with no competitive equivalent.

What it didn't do: resolve the capacity question. The data center thesis rests on a 2028 window with, today, one pilot line and a partial license at a partner whose SOP is 2029.

The next real catalyst is neither Honda nor a defense press release. It's either the target form factor announcement that unlocks the prepay, or a manufacturing partner for QSDC and QSAS. Until one or the other lands, the valuation rests on options, not on flows.
The post-earnings drawdown looks like a reaction to the cap headline by a market that never opened the 8-K. Cash mechanics are neutral, the prepay is intact, the 2029 SOP is reaffirmed. That doesn't make this quarter a blowout — but the structural thesis wasn't damaged by this amendment, it was repriced on a misread.

⑩ On sentiment, and where I stand.I've seen a lot of pessimism on X this week, and I understand the feeling that we're barely moving and that no objective is truly landing. But this kind of stretch is fairly common at a pre-revenue company — the gap between technical progress and anything the market can price is exactly where these names spend most of their life.

That said, management could do a lot better on clarity toward shareholders. Burying a CTO arrangement in the 10-Q rather than an 8-K is a choice, and it's the kind of choice that costs trust it didn't need to. And frankly, insider buying would be welcome — after this much selling, an open-market purchase would say more than any press release.

I haven't sold anything so far. On my Jan 2027 calls, I'll likely cut them on the next market bounce and roll into 2028 LEAPS — the thesis needs more runway than 2027 gives it.

President Donald Trump was handed a simple question aboard Air Force One on Monday. Where is the money?

"There's some reports that the United States has taken in $13 billion from Venezuela," one reporter began. "Where is that money going?"

An unidentified female reporter pressed on. "But where's that money going?"

Instead of answering, Trump once again compared himself to his predecessors. "No other president can say that for a long time," he said. "We had a cost.... We paid for it many, many times over."

The journalist wasn't having it. "But where is the money going?"

"It goes toward running the country," Trump finally helpfully said, before elaborating , "It can go to the military. Congress has to approve it .... We're taking in a lot of money. Billions and billions of dollars from Venezuela."

Of course, Trump never identified what account the money is being deposited into, what agency controls it, or under what legal authority it is being managed.

Because those questions matter. The Constitution gives Congress, not the president, the power to decide how federal money is spent.

Government revenue is ordinarily handled through established legal and budgetary processes, yet Trump offered no explanation of what sort of process he was referring to or whether he is even aware of them.

The exchange also comes as questions continue to grow over the fate of billions of dollars in Venezuelan oil proceeds now under U.S. control.

If Republicans lose control of the House, this issue should definitely be near the top of the hearings list.  Subpoenas of records and administration officials, and a demand for sworn testimony about where the money went and who has been controlling it.

Apollo Moves Up the Defence Value Chain with IPREK

Apollo has been empanelled by the Indian Air Force as a Prime Development Agency under the Make-II programme for the Indigenous Precision Range Extension Kit, or IPREK.

This marks an important shift in Apollo’s positioning—from being primarily a defence electronics and subsystem supplier to becoming a Prime Original Equipment Manufacturer responsible for complete system development and integration.

IPREK is designed to convert existing 500 kg unguided bombs into precision-guided glide weapons. The system is expected to offer a stand-off range of 80–100 km with accuracy of around three metres. This would allow aircraft to engage targets from safer distances while remaining outside the range of several air-defence systems.

Apollo’s entry into the Precision Guided Munition ecosystem is a structural positive. Recent global conflicts have highlighted the growing importance of long-range, accurate and cost-effective strike capabilities, making precision weapons one of the fastest-growing segments within defence.

The opportunity is also significant. The Defence Acquisition Council has approved defence procurements worth around ₹79,000 crore, with precision weapon systems among the key priorities. Apollo estimates that India’s import-substitution opportunity in this segment could exceed ₹20,000 crore over the next decade. The company has also referenced a global precision weapon systems market opportunity of nearly $10 billion by 2032.

IPREK brings together several advanced technologies, including NavIC-based satellite navigation, electro-optical guidance, infrared terminal guidance and Digital Scene Matching Area Correlation for operations in GPS-denied environments.

According to management, Apollo will own critical intellectual property related to the guidance software, flight computer and overall system-integration architecture.

While defence electronics typically generate attractive margins, complete precision-guided weapon systems offer substantially higher value addition. They also involve greater technological complexity, stronger pricing power and longer product life cycles.

Apollo’s selection as a Prime Development Agency therefore represents more than a single programme win. Successful development and delivery of IPREK could establish the company as a credible Prime OEM with proprietary guidance capabilities and open opportunities across future Army, Navy, Air Force and export programmes.

Laser air defenses will be operational before decade’s end, Lockheed exec says | Michael Marrow, Breaking Defense

The Pentagon should have high-energy lasers that can melt inbound aerial threats by 2030, a top Lockheed Martin executive told Breaking Defense.

“They’re here, they’re effective, and they are working,” Stephanie Hill, president of Lockheed’s rotary and mission systems division, said in an interview at the Farnborough Airshow on July 21. The company has successfully demonstrated “a number” of laser intercepts, she said, predicting that the directed-energy weapons would be ready for operations “before the end of the decade.”

Laser systems are often seen as a holy grail for air defense. They’re a cheaper way to knock down weapons like missiles and drones than the pricey interceptors the US has burned through in recent conflicts. The Pentagon has pursued defensive directed-energy weapons for years even as technical problems surfaced, but the potential upside has kept the department invested in solutions.

“If you have power[…] you have basically an infinite magazine,” Hill said. “So highly effective, highly cost-effective as well.”

An arm of Lockheed Martin earlier this month secured a major Pentagon contract to get some of those laser systems into the hands of troops. In parallel with the specialist firm nLIGHT, Lockheed under the Joint Laser Weapon System program will develop a prototype system with 150 kilowatts of power for “urgent operational demands,” which can then be scaled up to as high as 500 kW for cruise missile defense, the Pentagon announced. (The contract award did not specify a period of performance, and Hill did not comment directly on the program.)

Lockheed’s lasers use spectral beam combining technology, which has been demonstrated against small- to mid-size drones and “surrogate” cruise missiles at sea and on land, Hill said, using an industry term for a modified platform used to simulate enemy munitions. Referencing a common refrain that laser systems are always just five years away, Hill said, “Not anymore.”

While lasers weren’t debuted at the show, Lockheed last week unveiled two new systems aimed at lower-cost intercept solutions, including a cheaper version of its sought-after PAC-3 missile and an X-rotor system dubbed MORFIUS that can fly into drone swarms and fry them with a high-powered microwave.

The company is also offering an overarching system called Sanctum for defending military installations and civilian infrastructure from emerging drone threats, which Hill said uses an AI model to choose to employ different sensors and effects based on what type of threat is incoming.

Several European countries are also pushing for sovereign control over weapon systems as the continent ramps up defense spending. Hill emphasized Lockheed can support that desire with systems like Sanctum, including hardware and software.

“We can do that same thing with Sanctum if there are modifications that are needed for that country, or that country would want to have additional capability,” she said. “We understand that sovereignty and tech transfer is important, and we have solutions to be able to do that from a software perspective and a track record of being able to build workforce in other countries to deliver that.”

A Grizzly With ‘Pretty Much Everything’

Lasers would just be one element of what military officials have called a “layered” defensive system that they hope to build out across the force. Tim Cahill, chief of Lockheed’s missiles and fire control division, said during the interview with Breaking Defense that the company has tied in its Grizzly ground-based, containerized launcher with the Sanctum system to bring a wide range of interceptor options to bear.

“The intent for the containerized launcher approach is to have containers [with] everything from the smallest missiles we have all the way up [to] THAAD,” Cahill said. The Grizzly launcher, he added, “can be outfitted with pretty much anything, of any size.”

Using Sanctum and a Grizzly launcher armed with an AGM-179 JAGM, Cahill said the company “knocked down a Shahed surrogate” — referring to the low-cost kamikaze drone used extensively by Iran — in a recent demonstration.

“Our intent is to have a whole set of tools that we can bring in to adapt to whatever the situation is for a country,” Cahill said, similarly underscoring that sovereignty will be a key trait offered to foreign buyers.

An industry notice published by the Air Force July 17 is querying prospective vendors for a ground-based launcher that can defeat cruise missiles and drones of all types. At the time of the interview, Cahill said he had not yet had an opportunity to review the posting and its requirements, but said the Grizzly system could theoretically be a viable option.

“That is the intent, is that it is a multi-use [system], and it’s just a really simple little lid pop, raise up, and fire,” he said. “It just waits and does what it’s told, and goes.”

2026 Record Projection: 3–9

Best-Case: 6–6
UMass has a path to bowl eligibility if it handles Sacred Heart and Stonehill, wins key home conference games against Ball State and Akron, defeats Sacramento State on the road, and steals another MAC matchup against Eastern Michigan, Buffalo, or Bowling Green.

Worst-Case: 1–11
UMass enters the season with major efficiency concerns on both sides of the football. If the Minutemen fail to capitalize on their two early home games and continue struggling to sustain drives and prevent explosive plays, the season could quickly move toward another difficult finish.

Three Supporting Factors

1️⃣ Offensive production must improve substantially
UMass averaged only 3.6 yards per play, scored 0.146 points per play, converted 29.2% of its third downs, and finished scoring opportunities at a 61.9% red-zone rate last season. The Minutemen must become significantly more efficient to consistently finish drives.

2️⃣ The schedule provides several realistic opportunities
Sacred Heart, Stonehill, Ball State, and Akron represent UMass’ clearest chances to build its win total. Matchups against Sacramento State and Eastern Michigan could also become competitive if the Minutemen show early improvement.

3️⃣ Defensive consistency remains the biggest concern
UMass allowed 6.3 yards per play, 0.571 points per play, a 70.9% completion rate, and a 48.2% third-down conversion rate last season. Those numbers place considerable pressure on the offense and make it difficult to remain competitive over four quarters.

Key Swing Games

🏈 at Sacramento State — Sept. 26
A long road trip, but one of the more manageable games on the schedule. A win would give UMass momentum entering conference play.

🏈 vs. Eastern Michigan — Oct. 3
An important home MAC matchup and an opportunity to prove the Minutemen can compete against the middle of the conference.

🏈 vs. Ball State — Nov. 4
UMass’ best projected conference win opportunity and a game it likely needs to capture to reach three or four victories.

🏈 vs. Akron — Nov. 18
A late-season home game that could determine whether the Minutemen meet their projected record or fall below expectations.

Analysis

UMass enters 2026 projected near the bottom of the MAC, with an expected record of 3.1–8.9, a predictive ranking of No. 138 nationally, and a 14.3% chance of reaching bowl eligibility.

The schedule offers a manageable opening after the trip to Rutgers. Home games against Sacred Heart and Stonehill give the Minutemen two early opportunities to establish confidence before traveling to Sacramento State and beginning MAC play.

The largest concern is overall efficiency. UMass struggled to sustain drives last season, averaging only 3.6 yards per play and converting fewer than 30% of its third downs. Defensively, the Minutemen allowed opponents to complete more than 70% of their passes and convert nearly half of their third-down attempts.

The clearest path to three wins begins with Sacred Heart and Stonehill, followed by taking at least one game from Ball State, Akron, Sacramento State, or Eastern Michigan. Reaching the best-case scenario would require UMass to win nearly every favorable matchup and produce multiple conference upsets.

I project UMass to finish 3–9. The Minutemen should have opportunities to improve their record, but major offensive and defensive efficiency concerns make a bowl appearance unlikely.

text:
The Bloody Trifecta

How the Army of Tennessee Bled White Before It Ever Saw Franklin

They lifted him into the saddle every morning—two aides taking his weight between them, guiding the ruined leg into its accustomed place and lashing it fast with a leather strap, so that a man who could no longer stand unaided might still sit a horse and pass, for the length of a day, as a soldier in the field. The left arm hung from the shoulder in something like the shape of an arm, though it had done no useful work since Gettysburg and would do no useful work again for the rest of his life. Chickamauga had taken the leg. Two battles, less than three months apart, had between them cost him half a body, and he had bought both wounds leading from in front of the line and not from behind it—which was precisely the trouble, though nobody in Richmond seemed to see it yet.

Joe Johnston had spent two months and more falling back through north Georgia, trading ground for time the way he had always meant to fight this campaign—Dalton, Resaca, Cassville, Kennesaw, one delaying position after another, each of them costing Sherman more than it cost him, none of them a battle Johnston meant to stand and lose. It was a sound enough strategy for a general who understood the Confederacy could not replace what it spent, and a maddening one for a President who had never much cared for Johnston and liked him less with every mile of Georgia surrendered without the decisive fight Davis kept waiting for. By the middle of July, with Sherman across the Chattahoochee and Atlanta itself in plain sight, Davis ran out of patience for the war Johnston was willing to fight, and on the seventeenth he relieved him and handed the Army of Tennessee to John Bell Hood.

What Hood inherited, by the most careful counting available—Johnston's own return of July the tenth, the last full accounting taken before the axe fell—was fifty-nine thousand one hundred ninety-six officers and men present for duty. Not sixty-two thousand, whatever round number later attached itself to the moment; that larger figure—sixty-two thousand seven hundred forty-seven, to be exact—belonged to the return of June the thirtieth, three weeks and a bloody repulse at Kennesaw Mountain earlier, and armies do not hold still in the telling any more than they hold still in the field. Call it what it was: the Confederacy's second army, behind Lee's alone, worn some but not broken, handed now to a man who had never held a corps together for as long as it took his own men to carry him off it on a litter.

He was thirty-three years old, and there was no one in either army who seriously doubted his courage, nor much cause to doubt it: he had proved it at Gaines's Mill, at Second Manassas, at Antietam, at Chickamauga, in a war that had already used up most of the men who started it beside him in the old Texas Brigade. Davis and the war department jumped him over a long list of officers senior to him to give him the place, and gave him the rank of full general only as a temporary grade, tied to the command itself, as though even Richmond understood this was an experiment and wanted to keep the receipt. But courage was a virtue that scaled poorly upward. What a division needed from Hood—a fist thrown hard and straight, at a moment and place he chose for himself—was not what an army needed, which was patience, and cold arithmetic, and the harder gift of knowing when not to throw the fist at all. He had spent his whole career learning to be the hammer. Nobody had ever asked him to be the hand that decided whether to swing it, and so he swung it the only way he had ever been taught: hard, and often, and mostly at whatever stood in front of him. Davis had asked for a general who would fight. Hood meant to give him one, and it did not occur to him—or he would not let it occur to him—that a man might satisfy Richmond to the letter and ruin the army meant to carry the satisfaction out.

Sherman gave him the chance to prove it inside of three days. George Thomas's Army of the Cumberland was crossing Peachtree Creek in the sweltering third week of July, its three corps strung out and only partly over the water, cut loose for the moment from the rest of Sherman's converging columns—the best opening any Confederate commander would get in the whole campaign for Atlanta. Hood meant to hit it at one o'clock in the afternoon of the twentieth, while the gap in Thomas's line was still open. He did not hit it until past three, delayed by a corps that had to countermarch behind its own lines to reach position, and in those two lost hours Thomas's men dug, the way Federal soldiers in this war had gotten very good at digging, and the gap that might have decided a battle closed itself with shovels.

When Stewart's and Hardee's men went forward that afternoon it was into works that had not existed at one o'clock, across open pasture and through scrub timber with the July sun flat on their backs, Federal artillery finding the range early and holding it without much trouble after that. Twenty-five hundred Confederates fell in a few hours of fighting—the figure that has best survived the passage of time and the correcting of Federal exaggeration; Thomas, writing that night to report a victory, claimed a good many more, which was a habit of Union dispatches that whole summer, as though a fight not quite finished demanded a larger butcher's bill on the other side to make it feel finished after all. Hood had lost his chance in the space of an afternoon, and twenty-five hundred men along with it, and Sherman, reading the reports the next morning, understood something about his new opponent that would hold true for the rest of the campaign: this was a man who would attack, reliably, and not always wisely.

Two days later he tried again, and the design this time was better than the execution, which was fast becoming the pattern of Hood's command. Hardee took two full corps on a night march of some fifteen miles around the exposed left flank of McPherson's Army of the Tennessee, through country so choked with timber that units lost touch with each other in the dark and arrived on the morning of the twenty-second already used up before they had fired a shot. The surprise Hood needed was there to be had. The men meant to deliver it were too spent to deliver it well.

General W.H.T. Walker, riding ahead of his division to look over the ground, was shot dead by a Federal picket before the battle had properly begun—a division commander lost to one startled private's musket, in the careless way this war took generals as readily as it took privates, and with no more ceremony about it. On the other side of the field, a few hours later, James McPherson rode down a wooded lane alone to check his own lines and rode instead into a company of Confederate skirmishers who called on him to surrender; he wheeled his horse to run for it and was shot from the saddle, and was dead within the hour—the only commander of a full army, on either side, killed in action in the whole war. Sherman, told of it, could not at first speak, and then wept, for an officer he had called more than once the best young soldier in his command, and for a war that could take a man like that as casually as it took the nameless dead piling up on both sides of the field all that afternoon.

The fighting rolled on past McPherson's death into the evening, Cleburne's division doing what Cleburne's division nearly always did, breaking a Federal line and carrying guns it could not quite hold onto afterward. When it finally quit, Hood had spent fifty-five hundred men to gain nothing he could keep, against a Federal army that had lost its commanding general and something near three thousand of its own soldiers—a trade that looked, on the returns, almost even, and was not close to even at all, because armies never measure what they have lost only by counting rifles.

Six days after that, on the twenty-eighth, it happened a third time. Sherman was sliding west now, feeling for the one railroad still feeding Atlanta, and Hood sent Stephen D. Lee—new from Mississippi, commanding an infantry corps for the first time in his life—out to block him along the Lick Skillet road. What should have stayed a defensive fight, taken from behind whatever cover the ground offered, turned instead into a string of frontal assaults against breastworks that Logan's men had gone ahead and built, log by log, while they waited, the way Sherman's soldiers had learned to build faster than almost anyone else in that war. It was the most lopsided of the three fights. Many of Lee's men, veterans now of two hard battles inside of a week, went forward that afternoon into works they must have understood they could not carry, and did not carry, and paid for the trying without changing the shape of anything Sherman meant to do regardless. The Confederates lost somewhere near three thousand men. Logan's corps, fighting from behind its logs, lost a little over six hundred. Eleven thousand men, in eight days, in three battles that decided nothing Sherman could not have gotten anyway by patience—more than Joe Johnston had spent in the whole retreat from Dalton, sixty-odd miles and ten weeks of maneuver that Richmond had judged too timid to bear a moment longer.

On the thirty-first of July the returns came in, as they came in at the end of every month, war or no war, and a clerk somewhere behind the lines set down the figure that would follow this army through every retelling of the story afterward: fifty-one thousand, seven hundred ninety-three.

It is a number worth stopping over, because it has been put to work ever since as something it never was. Fifty-one thousand seven hundred ninety-three was the count of men present for duty—meaning they answered the morning roll, meaning they drew their rations, meaning the war department in Richmond could still enter that figure in a ledger and call it an army. It was not the count of men who could shoulder a rifle and stand in a line of battle against George Thomas's veterans, because present for duty swept in the teamsters and the cooks, the men laid up sick in the division hospitals, the details guarding bridges and depots thirty miles from the nearest picket line—all present, all counted, none of them available to Hardee on the morning a fight opened. Present for duty is the army as the paymaster counts it. Effective strength is the army the enemy actually meets. The two figures wear the same uniform in the official returns and mean entirely different things, and by the end of that July the gap between them in Hood's army had grown wide enough to hide a division in.

Call the next four months what the men who lived through them mostly called it: marching, and waiting, and marching again, broken now and then by the old violence. At the end of August, with Sherman's infantry finally astride the last rail line into the city, Hardee took two corps south to Jonesboro to save it and could not. The fighting ran two days, the thirty-first and the first of September, and on the second day the Federals found a thin stretch in Cleburne's line, broke through it, and walked around behind Brigadier General Daniel Govan's brigade and took it whole—Govan and several hundred of his Arkansas men marched off to a prison camp before most of them had fired more than a few rounds all day. Jonesboro cost the army close to three thousand more. It cost Atlanta as well; Hood pulled his army out of the city that same night, and Federal soldiers marched into it the following morning.

A month later, on the fifth of October, Sam French took his division north against a Federal supply depot at Allatoona Pass, held by a Union brigadier named John Corse who had reached the position with reinforcements only hours ahead of French's advance. French sent in the standard demand—surrender the works and spare the garrison further bloodshed to no purpose, in the formula nearly every such note used that war—and Corse sent back word that he meant to hold what he had, whatever it cost him. It cost both sides plenty. The fighting ran close around the redoubts for most of a morning, and when it ended French had lost close to nine hundred men taking a position he could not, in the end, afford to keep. His own report, filed a few days later, would only own to seven hundred ninety-nine—a discrepancy that says less about French's arithmetic than about a soldier's reluctance to write his own butcher's bill any larger than the facts strictly required.

Add to those two fights the slower bleeding of the weeks between and around them—a handful of men lost tearing up a water tank here, a handful more lost holding a bridge there, the small change of a war now being fought over Sherman's supply line instead of over Atlanta itself, no single clerk ever troubling to add the whole business into one clean total because no one action seemed worth a total at the time—and the combat bill for August, September, and October comes to something in the neighborhood of six thousand men. Not the ten thousand that later tellings have sometimes claimed. The larger figure, when it turns up, generally comes from counting the July fighting a second time, or from mistaking a monthly return for a butcher's bill, and the two were never the same thing and ought never to be added together as though they were.

The rest of what the rolls lost between the end of July and the third week of November went missing the way armies always bleed once the fighting stops being the whole story: men detailed away to hospitals and depots and never called back to their regiments; men whose year of enlistment simply expired, in an army that had stopped pretending by 1864 that such things mattered less than they once had; men down with the dysentery and the camp fevers that killed more Confederates in four years than Federal lead ever did; and men who, marching now through country some of them had been born in, stood their muskets against a fence rail some evening and walked home. The soldiers had their own name for it, half joke and half epitaph—a walking furlough, they called it, no leave papers required and no questions asked by anyone left with the authority to ask them. It was desertion by any name Richmond cared to give it, and it said something about the temper of an army that the enemy's bullets alone cannot be made to explain—something Hood, from the saddle he could no longer sit without help, chose for the most part not to see.

Set the two counts side by side and the shape of that whole autumn becomes plain enough, whatever quarrel a careful clerk might raise with the last exact digit. Fifty-one thousand seven hundred ninety-three present for duty on the thirty-first of July. Something between thirty-three and thirty-five thousand—Forrest's troopers counted in now—crossing the state line into Tennessee come the third week of November. Call the difference sixteen thousand men, call it seventeen; the two returns were not kept to quite the same standard, and an army that has stopped advancing keeps worse books than one that hasn't. But of that gap, the enemy's rifles and the enemy's prison stockades can be made to answer for something under six thousand. The rest—call it two men in every three the rolls lost that autumn—Hood lost without Sherman firing a shot at all.

While Hood's infantry bled away by that slower method, Nathan Bedford Forrest gave the Confederacy one more look at what audacity could do when judgment rode alongside it instead of standing in for it. In the last days of October he took his troopers up to the Tennessee River at Johnsonville, put guns on the bluffs above a Federal supply base that had never once imagined an enemy could reach it, and in an afternoon burned gunboats, transports, and several million dollars in Army stores before Federal reinforcements could organize any answer at all. It was the kind of clean, disproportionate victory Hood had spent the whole summer trying to manufacture with three infantry corps and had never once managed—a Confederate cavalryman asking the situation for everything it had to give, and getting it, because he had troubled to understand the situation before he acted on it. Forrest reached Hood at Florence in the middle of November with something over four thousand of his troopers, not all of them mounted and not the full strength Richmond had once promised, because even Forrest could not conjure horses that Alabama and Georgia no longer had left to give him. But he came. And Hood's arithmetic, for one more month, looked a little less desperate for his having come.

On the twenty-first of November, in a cold rain that would turn to sleet and then snow before the campaign was a week old, they lifted Hood into the saddle once more, strapped the dead leg fast against the stirrup, and pointed what remained of the Army of Tennessee north across the state line, toward Columbia and Spring Hill and Franklin, and toward an ending the arithmetic of that whole bled-white autumn had already gone a long way toward writing before a single Federal soldier fired a shot in Tennessee at all.

He had asked Richmond for the chance to attack, all the way back in July, and Richmond—glad of a general who still wanted to, after two years of generals who mostly hadn't—gave it to him, and kept giving it to him, every time he asked again. In four months of command, nobody in a position to stop him troubled to ask the one question that might have mattered more than any other: whether the army could survive being made to do everything Hood believed a Confederate general owed his president. He might, in fact, have answered that question more honestly than most men in his position could have. It was the one kind of arithmetic nobody had ever trained him to do, in a career built entirely on teaching him to do the other kind. He had learned, at Gaines's Mill and Second Manassas and Antietam and Chickamauga, exactly how to lead men into fire, and exactly what it cost him personally to do it—an arm, a leg, most of what a body has to give and still call itself a body. Nobody had ever taught him when to say that the price the army would pay could not be met. I get the MLS point a lot and I'll offer up some substantive thoughts. Again, I could be wrong, but I think MLS illustrates the point, not the rebuttal.

MLS can operate as the league-wide employer because it centralized the core player-employment relationship from the outset. The league owns the teams and player contracts, signs players, sets league-wide compensation and roster rules, and assigns players to clubs. Its investor-operators own interests in the league rather than conventional, independently owned clubs competing through a newly created umbrella entity.

It's when I try to retrofit that structure onto the SEC that the example exposes the problem.

Tennessee, Alabama, Georgia etc. are not franchises created by a central league. They are separate, preexisting public universities, owned by different states, governed by different boards, and accustomed to controlling their own recruiting, coaching, discipline, medical decisions, rosters, and player removal.

To approximate the MLS model, they would have to transfer substantial authority over those matters to the league. That is precisely the surrender of institutional control that I see no political will for AND which creates its own set of legal problems. In short, MLS does not show that the problem can be solved cosmetically. It shows how much control must actually be centralized. MLS had no independent clubs to preserve; the SEC is nothing but preexisting ones that intend to keep operating their own programs.

And it's at least worth noting that even MLS did not receive a clean single-entity exemption from antitrust law. In Fraser v. MLS, the First Circuit described the structure as a novel hybrid and resolved the case on the players' failure to prove the relevant market, rather than holding that MLS was categorically beyond Section 1. American Needle later reinforced the broader principle: calling an arrangement a single entity does not end the inquiry. The question is whether the challenged conduct combines otherwise independent centers of economic decisionmaking.

MLS also avoids two problems that are central to the college model. Its clubs are private, so it does not confront the NLRA-jurisdiction and sovereign-immunity issues created by state universities . And its structure did not create a union or a collective-bargaining relationship. The players organized through their own association and negotiated a CBA.

So yes, MLS is a model. But it demonstrates how much control the schools would have to surrender to replicate it—and how little the structure, standing alone, would solve.

Again, open to any and all pushback on this.

text:
[Take 8/15 · D-3]
### D-3. Meta reaches settlement with 52 US attorneys general on youth social media limits
*(as of 2026-08-27)*

**1. The Frame**

**What people think this is about:** Meta finally got caught for deliberately addicting kids to Instagram and Facebook, and a bipartisan army of state AGs forced the company to pay up big and install hard guardrails that will make social media safer for minors.

**What the machinery is actually doing:** A coalition of 51+ AGs extracted the largest Big Tech payout in history (~$12.7B guaranteed, up to $17–18B contingent) plus court-enforceable defaults on a company already under pressure, while Meta bought off the risk of a full trial verdict, massive damages exposure, and precedent without admitting liability. The deal sets industry-wide defaults that parents can override and ties tighter limits to competitors settling too.[[1]](https://t.co/RIpGRIpuWu)

**2. Observations**

- Bipartisan coalition of ~51 AGs (plus territories/DC) secured the headline win mid-trial; Meta avoided any admission of wrongdoing and paid a fraction of the ~$200B some states had signaled they would seek.[[2]](https://t.co/h9ruiIW354)
- Core relief is default 2-hour cumulative daily limit across FB+IG for under-18s (parental override only), midnight–6 a.m. block, school-hours notification mute (8 a.m.–3 p.m.), “productive pause” prompts every 15/60/90 minutes, hidden likes, banned cosmetic filters, and stronger age assurance—features Meta already had partial versions of in Teen Accounts.[[3]](https://t.co/IdZMPsEkP6)
- Payment structure is clever extraction: base ~$12.7B over 10 years + up to ~$5B more only if Snap/TikTok/YouTube match the terms. This creates direct incentive for competitors to settle rather than litigate.[[4]](https://t.co/a3bGDYFcMT)
- Florida AG rejected the deal as “peanuts” and vowed to continue litigating; Texas cut its own separate ~$1B deal. Not every state is on board, undercutting the “52 AGs unanimous” framing.[[2]](https://t.co/h9ruiIW354)
- Trial had only just begun (Aug 18 in N.D. Cal.); settlement came before key witnesses like Instagram’s Adam Mosseri finished testimony. States traded uncertain jury verdict for immediate, auditable changes and cash.[[5]](https://t.co/rmlTMgyPHe)
- No admission of guilt + parental override + DM exemption means the practical impact on highly motivated teens/parents is likely modest; the real product is precedent, cash for state programs, and pressure on the rest of the industry.

**3. Snapshot**  
On August 26, 2026, Meta announced (and a federal judge approved) a multistate settlement resolving claims by a bipartisan coalition of ~51 attorneys general (plus territories) that the company designed Instagram and Facebook with addictive features that harmed minors’ mental health and misled the public. The deal ends an ongoing federal trial in California that began August 18 and imposes default time limits, nighttime/school blocks, and other features on Meta’s platforms for users under 18, plus up to ~$17–18 billion in payments (partially contingent on other platforms). Meta denies wrongdoing.[[6]](https://t.co/9wYCI9nmSV)

**4. Timeline of material facts**  
- 2023: Multiple states file suits alleging Meta knowingly designed addictive features and misled the public (IT).  
- August 18, 2026: Federal trial begins in U.S. District Court, Northern District of California (LT).  
- August 26, 2026: Settlement announced and court-approved; Meta commits to defaults and payments (LT).  
- Same day: Florida rejects; Texas announces separate ~$1B deal (LT).  
- Ongoing: Limits subject to 5–10 year terms and independent auditor; contingent payments tied to competitor settlements (IT).

**5. Sides**  
**Coalition of ~51 AGs (bipartisan, IT/LT mix):** Steelman — States used consumer-protection authority to force concrete product changes and fund youth mental-health programs faster than a trial or legislation could deliver; the contingent structure pressures the entire industry toward safer defaults.  
**Critique:** LT — Claims of intentional design to addict and public deception remain unproven in court (Meta denies). IT — AGs secured cash and precedent without risking a loss or weaker remedy at trial; some states (Florida) view the payout as insufficient.

**Meta Platforms (IT dominant):** Steelman — Company already rolling out Teen Accounts and age tools; settlement lets it set industry standards on its terms, avoids existential damages, and preserves flexibility via parental overrides and DM exemptions while denying liability.  
**Critique:** LT — No admission means the underlying allegations of harm and deception are not judicially resolved. IT — Meta trades cash and defaults for litigation certainty and competitive positioning.

**6. Rumsfeld Matrix**  
- **Known Knowns:** Settlement terms (2-hour default, blocks, payments) are public and court-approved; Meta denies wrongdoing; trial was active.  
- **Known Unknowns:** Actual long-term compliance and behavioral impact on minors; whether TikTok/YouTube/Snap will match terms and trigger extra payments.  
- **Unknown Knowns:** Internal Meta data on efficacy of prior safety features and exact teen usage patterns that states used in negotiations.  
- **Unknown Unknowns:** Whether these defaults meaningfully reduce harm versus simply shifting usage to other platforms or workarounds; downstream effects on Meta’s ad revenue or teen mental-health trends.

**7. Incentives map**  
AGs gain cash for state programs, political credit on a popular issue, and precedent for future suits. Media gets a “Big Tech held accountable” narrative (high engagement). Meta buys certainty and shapes the new baseline. Competitors now face coordinated pressure to settle or litigate under worse optics. The money and defaults are the product; “protecting kids” is the framing that makes the extraction politically palatable.

**8. Dueling AI advice**  
**Moral AI Advice:** Defaults with parental override are better than nothing and create measurable friction, but they are not a substitute for actual parenting or addressing root causes of teen distress. Watch compliance data and competitor responses; the real test is whether usage drops or just migrates.  
**Evil AI Advice:** Perfect. Extract billions, lock in defaults that look tough but are easily bypassed by motivated users or parents, force rivals into the same box, and walk away with zero admission of fault. Rinse and repeat on the next platform.

**9. Practical takeaway**  
- Track the independent auditor’s first compliance reports (expected within months).  
- Watch whether Snap, TikTok, and YouTube announce matching terms— that triggers both tighter limits and the extra ~$5B.  
- States will decide how to spend the money; follow specific AG announcements for youth mental-health allocations.  
- For parents: the new defaults are on by default but reversible—test them.  
- Do not treat this as proof Meta “admitted” harm; it is a negotiated exit.  
- Monitor Florida’s separate litigation for any different outcome.

**10. What would falsify this read**  
- Court rejects the settlement or Meta walks away.  
- Major competitors refuse matching terms and the contingent payments never materialize.  
- Post-implementation data shows no measurable drop in teen usage or harm metrics (or a sharp rise in workarounds).  
- Internal documents released in ongoing litigation contradict the “no admission” framing with clear evidence of intentional deception.

Full Announcement:

Scientific Consortium Announces Potential Breakthrough in Sepsis and Infectious Disease

· Transplantation of mitochondria from platelets supercharges the immune system
· Synergistic combination with existing antibiotics
· Technology to be open sourced for use by any ER or hospital
· Has been in use, unrecognized, for over a century, in all platelet transfusions
· Most likely already covered by existing regulatory approval

------------------------

In 1928, Dr. Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin, leading to the era of antibiotics in medicine, saving countless millions of lives. Now, a consortium of top physicians and scientists from the US and Canada, working with startup Mitrix Bio Inc., have announced what promises to be another fundamental breakthrough for infectious disease, especially focused on sepsis. Sepsis annually causes the deaths of at least 350,000 adults and more than 1,800 children in the US alone, along with $62 billion in hospital costs, according to the Sepsis Alliance.

The new technique, called Platelet-Derived Mitochondrial Transplantation, uses components of platelets that have always been present in all blood and platelet transfusions but have remained unrecognized until now. Canadian scientist Dr. Eric Boilard discovered in 2014 that when platelets age or are intentionally activated, they eject their healthy mitochondria, encased in special extracellular vesicles (“Mitlets”). This is a natural process that results in the transfer of billions of mitochondria to the human bloodstream every day.

In hospitals and blood banks, donated platelets are commonly kept in storage for several days, ready for emergency use. During that time, the number of Mitlets floating free in the bag of platelets grows. Research has found that these Mitlets, when isolated from the platelets using a simple centrifuge spin, can be concentrated in large quantities and injected into patients safely and without bulky extraneous organic matter. In animal tests, this technique has produced major improvements in mortality and morbidity from sepsis, an otherwise extremely dangerous disease. This is a potentially powerful treatment for emergency rooms, hospitals, and even military field hospitals. The process should be tested in pilot studies in these locations.

Michael Snyder PhD, Chair of Genetics and Personalized Medicine at Stanford University, Chief Medical Advisor for Mitrix Bio, says: “This is an exciting development, coming after a lot of hard work by many teams, including here at Stanford. Mitochondrial transplantation is a growing field for many conditions, but sepsis is an especially important target because it’s so dangerous.”

How It Works

After they are separated from donated platelets, the Mitlets are injected intravenously into the target patient. The Mitlets are quickly absorbed by nearby white blood cells and other platelets. This leads to a “supercharging” effect, as the transplanted mitochondria boost the energy production of the recipient cell, allowing it to work harder and move faster to fight infection. Note that this is a natural process that already happens in the human body: platelets emit mitochondria, which are immediately absorbed and put to work by white blood cells. The transplant process simply isolates a much larger number of these Mitlets from donated platelets, potentially from younger donors, and then injects them into a sick patient to provide an extra immune-system boost.

Tom Benson, CEO of consortium leader Mitrix Bio, described it this way: “Imagine that you have a rechargeable drill, you’re working on a project, and the battery runs down. Your drill slows down. So, you plug in a freshly charged battery pack and complete the work. That’s what Mitlets do for immune cells…acting as replaceable battery packs, fresh energy boosts to keep the white blood cells working at top speed.”

This is a simple form of mitochondrial transfusion, an important new technique that has been tested by top researchers all over the world, with coverage in The Economist, Nature, Fortune, and other publications. Most conventional mitochondrial transfusions use mitochondria that are manually extracted from cells and are therefore fragile and short-lived. Mitlets, on the other hand, are naturally occurring, target white blood cells, and deliver mitochondria in protective capsules, making them an easier alternative.

Animal and Human Trials

This process was extensively tested in animal trials at the University of Kentucky and in human safety trials in Dallas, Texas. Now the team believes it should be tested more widely.

This technique has been used (albeit inadvertently) for decades, seemingly unknown to science. All platelet transfusions are, by definition, mitochondrial transplants, since the donated platelets release their Mitlets a few days after the transfusion, and any given unit of platelets contains large quantities of Mitlets in solution. Also, the practice of PRP (platelet-rich plasma) injections, which are performed at thousands of clinics nationally and internationally, effectively involves the transplant of mitochondria (Mitlets) as well.

“The new discovery that changes everything is that Mother Nature has been moving and swapping mitochondria around between cells for eons without our knowledge, so it turns out that doctors may have been doing the same without knowing it for a century,” says Lance Becker, MD, chair of emergency medicine for Northwell Health, a 23-hospital chain in New York, who is also organizing the annual Mitochondrial Transplantation International Conference in early 2027. “We hope that transferring or transplanting mitochondria by intention is going to have some important health benefit quickly, if we just figure out how to best use this new cellular and bioenergetic approach. ERs can start experimenting with it right away.”

Treatment Donated to Public Domain. Likely Pre-approved by Regulators

The isolation of these Mitlets from existing platelet donations is relatively simple, says the group. The protocol has been described in publications, and since it’s an extension of an existing process, it will be released as an “open-source” public-domain technique.

“This is a variation of a 100-year-old well-understood platelet donation process,” says Benson. “ER physicians and transfusion specialists have long suspected that platelet transfusions might benefit infections but didn’t fully appreciate the underlying mechanism. Now that we know it’s mitochondrial transplantation, we hope that clinicians can begin expanding standard-of-practice guidelines and learning how to best use it – a powerful new tool for doctors.”

Because it is an existing, if unrecognized, variation of platelet therapy, it is believed that this technique will likely be “grandfathered-in” by existing regulations. Mitrix and the consortium members stress, however, that there has been no formal legal determination of regulatory status, and anyone considering the process should consult with their own legal counsel.

Becker says, “Ideally, for a new medical treatment of this type, we want to create a small network of specialized research ERs in different parts of the nation to learn how to properly produce and administer the Mitlets, which will drive early human administration pilot studies for safety and feasibility. If possible, we will include VA and military medical researchers to learn more – faster – and to accelerate the pace of science. Doctors, clinicians, and patients striving for better health will need to drive it at the grass-roots level.”

The same immune-system boosting technique may also have benefits for many other diseases, including pneumonia, Covid, influenza, hospital-acquired infections, and potentially even cancer. Additionally, Mitrix Bio’s clinical partners in Right-To-Try 2.0 states will be offering the treatment for some conditions.

A New Approach to Infection Treatment

Eric Boilard, PhD, who is a Full Professor, Department of Microbiology and Immunology, Faculty of Medicine, Université Laval, and a scientific advisor for Mitrix Bio, says: “We have been very interested in the content and functions of these Mitlets.  Research in this field is advancing rapidly worldwide, and every new discovery is an exciting step toward understanding these remarkable particles and their potential impact on health and disease.”

Samir Patel, PhD, who is Assistant Professor, Department of Physiology, SCoBIRC at University of Kentucky, and also a scientific advisor for Mitrix Bio, says: "Mitochondrial dysfunction is one of the most underappreciated drivers of organ failure in sepsis – cells run out of energy faster than they can be rescued. Mitlets offer a way to address that energy crisis directly – a genuinely different lever from anything currently in the sepsis toolkit."

This new approach to infection treatment is not an antibiotic or an antiviral. It is an entirely new approach to fighting infection by supercharging the body’s own immune system.  It should be especially beneficial in the elderly, who have age-weakened mitochondria. The addition of new mitochondria from a younger donor can have the effect of making their immune system “younger.”

Note that the energy boost is temporary. After a few days, the new mitochondria are discarded along with the used-up and battle-damaged white blood cells. To extend the effect, clinicians may choose to do multiple treatments, perhaps every 2-3 days, until the sick/septic patient can be discharged from the ICU. Also, note that this technique seems to be perfectly compatible with existing antibiotics, providing the possibility of a synergistic “1-2 punch” for treating sepsis and other infections.

Potential Benefits

Sepsis claims 350,000 lives per year in the US and Canada, and it is one of the more expensive diseases for hospitals to treat. Assuming only a 20% improvement, a new treatment could potentially save 70,000 lives and $12 billion annually.

What’s Next

Tony. Fellow lawyer here. Start with Flint. This is an investigative lead for your office. If you want help, give me the subpoena results to analyze/expedite.  

Flint is the strongest presently documented DOL-related lead among the YC immigration companies because there are identifiable H-1B Labor Condition Applications under Flint Healthcare Inc., public representations that Flint coordinates PERM, prevailing-wage, and I-140 work, and a healthcare-placement model involving intended worksites away from Flint’s own office.

Flint currently markets a direct-hire healthcare placement and immigration-coordination program. It states that the healthcare facility is the employer and green-card sponsor, while Flint supports job matching, licensing, immigration processing, and relocation. Flint advertises approximately three-year commitments for registered nurses and physical therapists and approximately four-year commitments for other healthcare roles. Flint also publicly states that workers who voluntarily leave before completing the commitment may be required to repay costs incurred. [https://t.co/JahGASi0NJ] 

Flint’s Y Combinator posting for in-house immigration counsel states that the lawyer will file and oversee PERM labor certifications, prevailing-wage determinations, and I-140 forms. That establishes operational involvement in DOL-related filings. It does not establish which entity appears as employer or petitioner on any individual filing. [https://t.co/56fkjJd7Ka] 

A third-party compilation of OFLC disclosure data presently identifies 63 LCA records under Flint Healthcare Inc. for nursing positions at intended worksites in Alamogordo, New Mexico; Charlotte, North Carolina; Bainbridge, Georgia; Gunnison, Colorado; and Columbia, South Carolina. The records include critical-care, ICU, telemetry, operating-room, emergency-room, and behavioral-health nursing positions. Treat those figures only as leads. The compilation includes a denied case and later-withdrawn cases, uses calendar-year labels that do not correspond cleanly to OFLC fiscal-year reporting, and does not establish that a petition was approved or a worker was employed. Pull and reconstruct the official disclosure data and certified forms before relying on any total. [https://t.co/N3XCKvHpJ3]

The investigation should proceed on separate tracks.

The H-1B track is a DOL matter. Determine whether Flint was the bona fide H-1B employer; whether every actual place of employment and secondary entity was accurately disclosed; whether Flint paid the greater of the applicable actual or prevailing wage; whether workers were paid during employer-caused nonproductive time, including licensing, credentialing, and placement delays; whether required worksite notice and Public Access Files were maintained; and whether Flint or a facility recovered employer business expenses or imposed an unlawful early-termination penalty.

The standard-PERM track applies to LPNs, CNAs, medical assistants, and other non-Schedule A roles. Determine which facility filed each ETA-9089, whether the permanent job was genuine and available, whether recruitment was conducted in good faith, whether U.S. applicants were lawfully considered, and whether prohibited labor-certification expenses were shifted to the worker.

The Schedule A track applies to qualifying professional nurses and physical therapists. Those applications are filed with USCIS rather than an ETA processing center. Obtain the complete I-140 Schedule A files through USCIS or an interagency request, including the prevailing-wage determination, Notice of Filing, ETA-9089 materials, professional qualification evidence, permanent-job offer, and ability-to-pay evidence. The absence of a Flint-named case in OFLC’s ordinary PERM disclosure data does not establish the absence of Schedule A sponsorship.

It is not inherently improper for Flint to be the temporary H-1B employer and a healthcare facility to be the prospective permanent employer. The issue is whether the same-worker records disclose a genuine temporary employment relationship followed by a genuine permanent job, or instead show a false employer, false worksite, sham job offer, wage violation, or materially inconsistent representations to DOL and USCIS.

First document pull:

1. The complete OFLC LCA disclosure rows, worksite appendices, secondary-entity fields, certified ETA-9035/9035E forms, and status histories for all Flint Healthcare Inc., Flint, With Flint, DBA, predecessor, successor, and related-entity filings. Search by legal name, address, responsible official, attorney or agent, and FEIN, not name alone.
2. The corresponding I-129 petitions, approval or denial notices, beneficiary crosswalk, actual employment start and end dates, and any amended petitions. An LCA without an approved and used petition should be separately identified.
3. The Public Access File for each LCA, including the certified LCA, wage-rate statement, actual-wage methodology, prevailing-wage source, benefits statement, and evidence of notice at each third-party worksite. Public Access Files must be maintained for public examination, although underlying payroll is obtained separately in enforcement.
4. Payroll, timekeeping, benefits, deductions, reimbursements, W-2 data, bank-payment records, assignment records, licensing dates, credentialing dates, and all periods without an active facility assignment. Compare payment not merely to the stated LCA wage, but to the greater of the applicable actual and prevailing wages.
5. Every Flint-facility placement, staffing, direct-hire, immigration-support, or services agreement. Identify who selected and supervised the worker, assigned shifts and duties, evaluated performance, controlled leave, paid wages and benefits, disciplined or terminated the worker, bore the cost of nonproductive time, and could transfer the worker to another site.
6. Every worker-facing offer letter, H-1B agreement, green-card sponsorship agreement, commitment agreement, promissory note, relocation agreement, wage-deduction authorization, repayment schedule, and collection communication. Identify every worker from whom repayment was demanded or received and the component costs included in the demand.
7. For non-Schedule A roles, the complete DOL PERM file under the facility petitioner’s name, including prevailing wage, ETA-9089, recruitment report and evidence, applicant dispositions, Notice of Filing, audit materials, and payment records. For Schedule A cases, obtain the complete USCIS I-140 package rather than looking for an ordinary OFLC PERM disclosure record.
8. All attorney engagement letters and Forms G-28. Identify the client or clients, fee payer, preparer, scope of representation, conflict disclosures, and whether Flint’s in-house or outside lawyers represented the facility, Flint, the worker, or multiple parties.

The immediate public-record test should be a representative PAF request covering the 2026 Alamogordo filing and a sample from each earlier worksite. That will not establish payroll compliance, but it will identify the asserted actual-wage system, prevailing-wage source, worksite notice, benefits treatment, and the employer’s documented compliance architecture.

text:
Vitamin D Linked to 13% Cognitive Boost in Early Dementia, Study Shows | Peter Dockrill, ScienceAlert

For anybody with a loved one experiencing dementia or Alzheimer's, news of prospective drug treatments failing or producing mixed results is a cause for concern.

But emerging evidence gives reasons for hope too, with research suggesting a common vitamin supplement may have a promising effect on patients with signs of early dementia, and it's a cheap daily pill that's available to anybody.

In a new study published in Sleep Medicine, scientists found daily intake of a vitamin D supplement was linked with a significant boost in cognitive test results for people with two hallmarks of early dementia: mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and sleep disturbances.

According to the scientists, it's the first research analyzing the link between vitamin D supplementation and cognition in patients with these two key symptoms, but it's worth noting that this is only a small observational study – and it doesn't prove that vitamin D enhances cognitive performance.

Nonetheless, the findings add to growing evidence that vitamin D may protect brain health and help stave off dementia, in addition to seemingly offering benefits to aging processes, heart health, and depression, among many other conditions.

As we so often see with neurodegenerative diseases, taking action early may be crucial, researchers think.

"This may represent a critical window for intervention, when cognitive changes are emerging, but opportunities to support brain health may remain," says sleep scientist Victoria Pak from Emory University in Atlanta, Georgia.

In the study, Pak's team assessed 54 adults aged 50 or older, all of whom had diagnosed or suspected MCI, and showed signs of sleep disturbance.

The participants undertook the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) to evaluate their levels of cognitive function, and two separate tests to measure their sleep quality, the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS).

Participants also reported their levels of vitamin D intake, and when the researchers compared their daily dosage against the cognitive and sleep measures, an interesting result stood out.

After accounting for potential confounding factors including age, sex, body mass index (BMI), vitamin D type, and education level, the researchers found participants who took a daily dosage of 5,000+ IU of vitamin D scored ~13 percent higher (3.78 points higher) on the MoCA cognitive test results compared with those who didn't take vitamin D supplements.

People taking lower daily doses of vitamin D also scored nominally higher than participants who didn't take daily vitamin D, but the lower-dose results were not statistically significant.

The association for 5,000+ IU held true regardless of whether the participants took vitamin D2 or vitamin D3, but it's worth noting that 5,000+ IU is slightly above the maximum suggested daily intake of vitamin D, which is 4,000 IU, an amount generally considered to be the safe upper limit to avoid developing hypercalcemia.

For that reason, it's important to realize that the key result here is not any kind of updated recommendation about how much vitamin D people should take – even if research is starting to show that doses between 4,000 and 6,000 IU may offer greater protection against some adverse health outcomes.

At this stage, this is only a preliminary finding from a small study, which the researchers say warrants further analysis in subsequent studies involving larger groups of participants.

While we have to remain cautious for now, it's a great lead for scientists to investigate in future, especially since vitamin D is so inexpensive and readily available.

Once the science settles, we could have something really significant here.

"Identifying accessible and modifiable factors, such as vitamin D supplement intake, during the earlier stages of cognitive decline may become increasingly important," Pak says, "particularly as rates of Alzheimer's disease continue to rise."

text:
Tax Abatements Are Becoming a Multi-Billion Dollar AI Line Item

Tax abatement deals represent a distinct form of public spending. Instead of writing a company a check, a government agrees to collect less property, sales, or other tax revenue, usually in exchange for investment, jobs, or another public benefit.

The traditional model centers on economic development. Bexar County, Texas approved an estimated $16.4 million incentive, an 85 percent property tax abatement through 2038, for a $700 million expansion of H-E-B’s San Antonio operations. H-E-B committed to 720 jobs by 2030. The unresolved question in deals like this is whether the company would have built the project anyway. 

Research on large firm-specific incentives has found they can boost employment in the targeted industry but weaker evidence they lift broader county or state growth, with one study finding an average cost around $120,000 per promised job.

AI data centers have turned this into a much larger fiscal question. At least 38 states offer incentives targeting data centers, provisions often written before AI-driven capital spending reached its current scale. EdgeConneX is developing a roughly $1.4 billion data center campus in Bastrop County, Texas, under a 10-year property tax abatement. 

Washington State’s legislative auditor found beneficiaries of an urban data center tax preference saved an estimated $42.4 million from 2023 to 2026 while generating just 53 family-wage jobs, and that the incentive was largely used for refurbishment rather than attracting new projects.

Good Jobs First, a group critical of corporate subsidies, estimated roughly $2.5 billion in projected fiscal 2026 revenue losses in Georgia, $1.3 billion in Texas, and $1.94 billion in combined state and local losses in Virginia. Ohio’s governor paused its data center exemption for new applicants after the state reported losing about $1.6 billion in 2025. These figures come from an advocacy group rather than a neutral accounting agency, but they point to a structural problem: incentives written for smaller conventional data centers now apply to hyperscale campuses worth many times more.

Transparency compounds the issue. A direct grant of $50 million is visible on a budget line. Forgiving $50 million in taxes over 15 years can carry a similar fiscal effect while remaining far less conspicuous, and Good Jobs First argues many jurisdictions still underreport these losses.

Abatements are not limited to corporate subsidies. Chattanooga, Tennessee ties the size of its affordable housing tax abatement directly to the cost of the units produced. Ulster County, New York approved a 50 percent property tax exemption for qualifying low-income homeowners in subsidized homes. 

Buffalo’s $225 million Canalside development, by contrast, received a 30-year abatement whose value has not been publicly disclosed, far longer than typical local deals.

Energy infrastructure adds another layer. Houston approved an $11 million, 10-year abatement for a $570 million NRG natural gas peaker plant, waiving its own rule against incentives for power generation. The project promises 455 megawatts of capacity but only 14 permanent jobs, alongside a $21 million school district tax break and a $370 million low-interest state loan.

Each of these deals invites the same underlying question: whether a government is purchasing something with foregone tax revenue that it could not have obtained otherwise, and whether the public benefit matches what was surrendered to secure it.
