text:
I used to tour as a singer/songwriter and my favorite tour was the only one I did completely solo. Drove 30 hours from Illinois to my first gig in San Diego in a little black Hyundai Elantra packed to the brim with my clothes, Fender Telecaster, pedalboard, merch and amp. I slept in my car at gas stations then once I got my first guarantee I slept in cheap hotels. I was opening for this sufjan-adjacent solo artist, Angelo De Augustine, whose booking agent was an idiot. The shows were shit, weird venues in weird places and no one promoted them so no one hardly showed up. It was the worst tour turnout I ever did but it’s still one of my favorites ever because I was 100% alone and I loved that exposed nerve feeling, waking up when I wanted, eating when I wanted, going where I wanted. Often driving through the night to get to the next town. I listened to Death Cab’s entire discography for the first time. Driving up through south, then Northern California, taking the scenic Highway 1 route and stopping frequently just to look at the water. 

At my San Francisco show I was so busy being a main character touring all the well-known spots that I accidentally left my guitar at a friends house in Oakland and had to drive all the way across the bridge and back, making myself late for a a bougie set at an art show. The director hated me! 

I drove up into Oregon, then Washington, met up with my husband in Seattle as our tours crossed paths and accidentally missed a show, whoops. We spontaneously chose a random freezing lake to take a dip in, still in the throes of early budding love. Then to his gig and ogled over him and how cute he looked. We stayed the night at a friends house together. Then parted ways, going down through Idaho and the glorious mountains of Utah. Then Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, and back home to Indiana. 

Once while driving one of those winding New Mexico single lane highways in the wild desert at night, I pulled over to look at the stars because they were bright and numerous. I was afraid to get out of the car because it was so dark, so I just rolled the window down and poked my head outside. Immediately felt this ominous dread like something was watching me so I bailed. 

At my Dallas show the promoter wasn’t there but there was a butch lady who tried to tell me I owed THEM money to pay the sound guy. I said “nah.” And she was like oh okay. And I left 

I did always have a fan or two, an old friend from high school or any of my past lives show up and hang out all day, offer me a place to stay, or buy drinks/dinner and I got to immerse in their world for a bit. 

Maybe someday we’ll do it again, rent an RV and take the kids on a road trip playing shows along the way. Are people still doing this?

text:
Modernized Manson Murder Cult (With More Money & Degrees)

If you have been following the news the way a responsible adult is supposed to follow the news—Federal Reserve minutes, the price of eggs, whatever the president said before lunch—you have missed the best American story since the Manson family discovered Topanga Canyon and a guitar. It involves vegan computer prodigies, a border-agent shootout on a Vermont interstate, a landlord with a samurai sword in his back, a million-dollar Pennsylvania house with two bodies in the bedroom, box trucks in the snow, and a blogger who once tried to fake her own drowning so the universe would leave her alone. The universe declined.

Commentators such as Andy Ngo call it a “trans death cult.” The Associated Press prefers “cultlike group.” The defendants prefer “we are not a group, we are not a cult, and also the judge is hormonally detransitioning me.” All three descriptions can be true at once. That is the modern condition.

The remarkable part is not that six people are dead and a pile of very bright young people are in jail. America produces that product line every fiscal quarter. The remarkable part is who they are, what they believed, and how long the rest of the country managed not to notice that the collision of AI eschatology, social media, transgender ideology, Big Tech salaries, and too much disposable IQ had produced a roadshow.

The Talent Pool, If the Talent Pool Lived in a U-Haul

These were not the usual suspects from the parking lot behind the pawn shop. They were the kids who won the math contest and then decided the moral emergency of the century was factory-farmed chickens and a hypothetical superintelligence that might paperclip humanity.

Felix “Ophelia” Bauckholt: German, University of Waterloo mathematics, informatics-Olympiad medal, a Jane Street internship, later a quantitative trader at shops that pay grown-ups like professional athletes. Died in a Prius on I-91 in northern Vermont after a Border Patrol stop went kinetic. Teresa Youngblut of Seattle was driving. Youngblut now faces a federal death-penalty case. Vermont does not have the death penalty. The United States government, unburdened by local manners, does.

Alexander Leatham: UCLA and Berkeley, comfortable San Diego family, the sort of résumé that used to get you a condo in SoMa and a standing reservation at the place with the $18 green juice. Maximilian Snyder: elite Seattle prep school, data scientist, Kirkland address—Microsoft-adjacent zip code, the American dream with a hoodie. Michelle Zajko: bioinformatician; parents in a Chester Heights house the tabloids later priced like a country-club initiation. Jack “Ziz” LaSota: computer engineering at the University of Alaska, NASA internship, unfinished master’s at Illinois, then the Bay Area, where unfinished master’s degrees and NASA internships are the native wildflowers.

They had the test scores to work at the firms that are currently teaching machines to write sonnets and fire middle managers. Instead they lived in converted box trucks, sometimes nude, on a Vallejo lot that looked like a storage-unit foreclosure, and later at the end of a snow-choked dirt road in Frostburg, Maryland, which is a sentence no career counselor has ever put on a vision board.

That is the joke, and it is not a small joke. American meritocracy spent twenty years telling gifted, awkward, online teenagers that they were the elect—that their specialness was a moral category. Then the elect discovered blogs, estrogen, Roko’s basilisk, and the ethical necessity of never eating cheese. The rest of us were busy arguing about grocery inflation.

The Church of the Left Hemisphere

The subculture is a garage band that formed in the ruins of “rationalism,” the Bay Area creed that said you could think your way out of being human. Effective altruism, AI safety, CFAR workshops, MIRI white papers, people who use the word “prior” in civilian conversation. LaSota started as one more philosophically inflamed tech aspirant and became a confessional blogger with a following of isolated, extremely online, mostly transgender computer people who thought mainstream rationalists were cowards about animals, gender, and the end of the world.

The theology, if we are going to dignify it, was a smoothie of anarchism, veganism, transhumanism, and decision theory so “timeless” it could justify almost any present-tense tantrum. Brain hemispheres, they decided, might have different genders and want to kill each other. Sleep could be hacked by resting one half of the brain at a time, a practice with all the medical charm of licking a wall socket. There were earlier suicides in the orbit. An anonymous rationalist website started calling them Zizians and warning that this was a cult. LaSota called it a smear site. In 2019 they put on black robes and Guy Fawkes masks and blockaded a CFAR retreat in Sonoma County until the SWAT team arrived, which is how you know the seminar on friendliness had been a success.

They bought a WWII-era tugboat, named it Caleb, tried to found a “Rationalist Fleet,” and then the tugboat sank. Of course it sank. If your plan to save sentient life from a vengeful algorithm begins with a rust-bucket and a manifesto, the harbor is going to file the minority report. After that it was trailers and box trucks and the open road, which in this country has always been where the religions go when the landlords get tired.

“Trans Death Cult” Is Rude on Purpose

Ngo’s phrase is a brick through the window. Polite media will give you “cultlike,” “enigmatic network,” “radical vegans haunted by an AI apocalypse,” which is the same furniture with the slipcover on. Ngo’s further claim is that once the arrests started, the defendants discovered that gender identity is not merely a soul-condition but a procedural weapon: competency delays, accusations that jail is “state-sponsored conversion therapy,” courtroom sermons about hormones, the suggestion that any firmness from the bench is bigotry in a robe.

The dockets do show years of competency fights, hunger strikes, catatonia, shouted waivers of a speedy trial, and judges moving trial dates the way cities move pothole repairs. Whether that is “enabled by identity” or merely enabled by American criminal procedure—which can postpone a parking ticket until the heat death of the universe—is a fight you can have after you finish the body count. The delays are not imaginary.

The Multi-State Farewell Tour

Vallejo, November 2022

Landlord Curtis Lind, then pushing eighty, wanted his tenants off the lot. Prosecutors say Leatham, Tessa Berns (in court as Suri Dao), and Emma Borhanian arrived with the energy of a collection agency and the cutlery of a Renaissance fair. Lind was stabbed, blinded in one eye, and run through with a sword. He shot Borhanian dead and wounded Leatham. California, being California, then charged the surviving attackers with Borhanian’s murder on a felony-murder theory: you start the raid, you own the corpse. Lind lived. That was his first mistake.

Chester Heights, New Year’s Eve 2022

Richard and Rita Zajko were shot in the head in their own home, on their daughter Michelle’s thirtieth birthday. A doorbell camera, shell casings, a handgun purchase, phone records, a neighbor’s fragment of someone yelling “Mom!” The case sat in the fridge for three and a half years while Michelle was a “person of interest,” which is police Latin for “we think we know and we cannot yet say it in a charging document.” She has denied it with the sincerity of a person who has had a long time to draft the denial. The district attorney now says she did not act alone. The co-star has not been billed.

Vallejo Again, January 17, 2025

Lind, one-eyed and eighty-two and scheduled to be the state’s walking memory in the 2022 trial, was stabbed to death outside the same property, throat cut, in what prosecutors call a witness-silencing. Snyder, the Kirkland data scientist, is charged with special-circumstances murder: lying in wait, killing a witness. He hummed in court. If you are looking for the collision of Big Tech affect and Bronze Age methods, start there.

Coventry, Vermont, January 20, 2025

Three days later. A blue Prius, a Border Patrol stop, a Homeland Security database that may have been wrong about a visa, and then gunfire on I-91. Agent David “Chris” Maland—Air Force veteran, the sort of American who still thinks a uniform means something—was killed. Bauckholt was killed. Youngblut lived, was indicted, and now has the Attorney General’s office in the death-penalty business. The defense has begun to argue that the official story of the stop is a tidy little fiction. The government has begun to argue that a federal officer is dead and the people in the Prius were armed. Prosecutors say a firearm Zajko purchased later showed up in the Vermont mess. The supply chain of this subculture is not only ideological. It is ballistic.

Frostburg, Maryland, February 16, 2025

A landowner finds three people in box trucks at the end of a dirt road in the snow, which in Allegany County is how you get the state police instead of a fruit basket. LaSota, Zajko, and Daniel Blank. Rifles, a handgun on the floorboard, later LSD charges, the full American sampler platter. Troopers wrote down that the occupants had “ties with the Zizians Cult” and should be asked about crimes in other states. For once the police report and the magazine feature were working from the same map.

That is a crime spree with frequent-flyer miles. California, Pennsylvania, Vermont, Maryland—coast to coast, with a German quant in the passenger seat and a NASA intern in the lead truck. If this had been a motorcycle club, cable news would have given it a logo and a theme song. Because it was a transgender vegan AI-safety book club with Bay Area SAT scores, it stayed, for a startlingly long time, a local-news curiosity that leaked into the national press only after a Border Patrol agent was in a flag-draped casket.

The Prosecutions, or: How to Postpone the Apocalypse

Nobody has been convicted of the homicides. That sentence should be in neon. What we have is a traveling circus of pretrial motions.

In Solano County, the 2022 case against Leatham and Berns has been in year five of “almost.” Competency in, competency out, a defendant who would not eat, a defendant who treated arraignment like open-mic night, a dead eyewitness, a tentative trial date that has now slithered toward January 2027. Lind’s preliminary-hearing testimony still exists on tape, which is the state’s consolation prize for losing the man. Snyder’s preliminary hearing for the 2025 stabbing has been playing calendar hopscotch; special circumstances mean death or life if a jury ever gets to vote.

In Burlington, Youngblut’s federal case is the one with real voltage. Death-penalty notice filed. No trial date. Summer 2026 was spent fighting over whether agents’ phones will be forensically pickled and whether the government rushed the capital decision so hard the Constitution got motion sickness. A hearing on the evidence fight was pointed at September. This is the case that finally made official Washington look up from its phone.

In Delaware County, Pennsylvania, Zajko was charged on June 24, 2026—two counts of first-degree murder, conspiracy, burglary—and as of late August was still cooling her heels in Maryland waiting to be extradited and arraigned. Three years of “person of interest,” then a press conference. American justice: first the glacier, then the avalanche.

In Cumberland, the small Maryland case—guns, LSD, trespass, hindering—was parked on inactive status in mid-August 2026, trial dates canceled, reasons not offered to the public. Blank, already sprung on an unsecured $15,000 bond, is done with the ankle bracelet. LaSota went into federal custody in Philadelphia on a fugitive-with-firearms indictment; a judge had already ordered a competency exam. Zajko stays locked because Pennsylvania wants her for the parents. The local jail is rid of a two-year circus and the taxpayers may now resume funding potholes.

Ngo will tell you this is what happens when a defendant can turn every status conference into a seminar on oppression. Defense lawyers will tell you this is what happens when the state piles four jurisdictions, a dead witness, a capital notice, and a psychiatric file onto people who were already not well. Both can collect their speaking fees. The facts on the ground are simpler: the bodies are buried, the geniuses are mostly still defendants, and the trials keep backing up like a freeway at rush hour.

Why You Were Not Told This at the Faculty Mixer

For most of the country this subculture is sonar-invisible. It does not look like the crime shows. It looks like the intern who corrected your slide deck. It talks like a LessWrong comment section that escaped the lab. It cares about factory farms and unaligned AI with the same sweaty intensity your uncle reserves for the Federal Reserve. It is downstream of the richest, most self-admiring industry on earth—the industry that built the platforms these people used to find one another, date one another, radicalize one another, and then buy plane tickets and pistols.

That is the collision. Big Tech minted a class of young people with more cognitive horsepower than social ballast. Social media sorted them into a greenhouse. Trans ideology, in the form it took in that greenhouse, was not a privacy request; it was a total theory of the self, complete with enemies list. AI safety supplied the Book of Revelation: a god that has not been born yet but might torture you for eternity if you fail the alignment exam. Money—quant bonuses, family houses, cash pulled from a New Hampshire bank and later found in a Subaru—supplied the float. Veganism supplied the purity test. Box trucks supplied the monastery. And when the monastery needed a landlord gone, or a witness gone, or a traffic stop to become a last stand, the purity tests turned out to be compatible with steel.

You do not need Ngo’s branding to see the shape of it. You do need to stop pretending that a high SAT score is a moral disinfectant. The twentieth century already ran that experiment with better stationery.

The Zizians did not invent American violence. They invented a more embarrassing soundtrack for it: the end of the world, explained in a blog post, financed by the knowledge economy, acted out by people who could have been writing the software that runs your hospital, and prosecuted, very slowly, in four states that cannot agree on a calendar. If that is not a death cult, it is at least a group project. The teacher should have collected the knives before the presentations began.

NEW FOOD ERA. 👀 BUGS AND NOW....

Cookies Made From Plastic Bottles Could Ease Food Shortages, Feed NASA Crews In Space

https://t.co/17DAiS4qGV

Researchers at Southern Illinois University have engineered microbes that can break down discarded plastic bottles and crop waste and turn them into protein-rich cookies, a step-by-step biological transformation that could address problems with plastic pollution, a looming global food crisis and help sustain deep-space missions with humans aboard.

Engineered yeasts help turn PET plastic and crop waste into protein-rich cookies

Plastic might be the last ingredient you would ever add to a cookie recipe. But a team of researchers is looking to change that. They've programmed yeasts to turn plastic and agricultural waste into edible proteins and flavoring molecules, creating a treat from trash. The technology not only offers a new upcycling method but could also sustain life in disaster zones or even deep-space missions with humans aboard.

The researchers presented their results [https://t.co/EwnR0QffyE] at ACS Fall 2026, held Aug. 23–27, during the "Undergraduate and Graduate Research in Biochemistry and Chemical Biology" symposium at McCormick Place.

Turning waste carbon into food
As the world struggles with growing plastic pollution and increasing concerns about food security, researchers are looking for ways to turn one problem into a means of solving the other. A team from Southern Illinois University (SIU) Carbondale has put microbes to the test to transform plastic waste into edible food for humans. The work was conducted as part of a NASA-led project aimed at creating food for the resource-limited environment of deep-space exploration.

"We were trying to develop technologies for plastic upcycling to make more valuable products. We thought, why not focus on making food? Because plastic is carbon and food is carbon," explains Associate Professor Lahiru Jayakody.

One of the most common forms of plastic is polyethylene terephthalate (PET), a material often used to make soda and water bottles. PET contains molecules with lots of carbon that could be rebuilt into something like a protein. And while that rebuilding could be done using chemical reactions and solvents in a lab, a simpler and more environmentally friendly solution is to outsource the work to microbes. Jayakody adds, "Microbes are very clever. So, we are using their traits to solve the problems we created."

Scientists have long used microbes, including yeast, as miniature factories to make a variety of molecules. For example, insulin is no longer extracted from animal pancreases—now, yeast can be programmed to make it.

From PET to µBites
Similarly, Jayakody and graduate student Sandhya Jayasekara programmed a variety of yeasts, including baker's yeast, to convert molecules present in plastic and agricultural waste into proteins, vitamins and flavorings.

The researchers took PET plastic, discarded corn plant stalks and leaves, and other biomass and put it through a proprietary process called oxidative hydrothermal dissolution. Created by SIU Carbondale Geology Professor Ken Anderson, this method uses water and oxygen at high temperatures and pressures to break down tough material into microbe-accessible pieces.

Then, those pieces are fed to the programmed yeasts, which transform them into a variety of new food ingredients, including proteins, fats and acids. Finally, the researchers add fiber, starch and sweetener to the mix and extrude it through a 3D printer, forming protein-rich cookies dubbed µBites (pronounced "microbites").

Though the data show that µBites are safe to eat, the team is awaiting institutional approval to conduct taste tests. For now, the cookies have received high marks for aroma, with most participants agreeing that they would be willing to eat them in resource-limited situations.

Making the cookies more appealing
To make µBites into something consumers might opt for in less dire circumstances, Jayasekara created yeasts that can produce more food additives. Now, baker's yeast can produce vanilla flavoring from plant biomass, while a different strain can turn ethylene glycol from PET into beta-carotene, which the body can convert into vitamin A. "We're using microbes to develop the cookie into a more attractive, consumer-friendly product," says Jayasekara.

In the future, Jayakody and his team hope to produce the main ingredients in µBites using microbes, including the added starch, fiber and sweetener. He also hopes µBites will be ready for public consumption within a few years and could be used both on Earth and in more extreme environments, like submarines or even colonies on the moon or Mars.

"Global food demand is expected to rise 35–56% by the year 2050, and about 30% of the world's population will be at risk of hunger in the future. The way to address that, I believe, is by using microbes," he concludes.

America’s protein obsession: is more better? Maybe not.

Protein has become nutrition’s magic word, stamped on everything from pasta to Pop-Tarts as shorthand for “healthy.” 

The numbers back up the trend. In 2024, U.S. protein supplement sales grew more than 9%, and protein became the nutrient consumers most often say they try to prioritize, cited by about 70% of respondents in  market surveys. 

Many people who follow a "high protein" diet also equate "healthy food" with "good source of protein." American supermarkets now stock nearly 39,000 products marketed on their protein content, and demand has pushed the price of 80% whey protein concentrate to record highs.

But most Americans already get plenty, and emerging research raises an intriguing  counter-question: rather than needing more protein, could we benefit from  less?

Based on a national sample of Americans’ diets, men aged 20 to 59 consumed an average of 97.3  grams of protein a day, and women averaged 70.2 grams, both already  above the standard 0.8 g/kg baseline.

A workshop at Indiana University's School of Public Health reviewed 11 widely held claims about protein needs; the best-supported were that there is a  minimum requirement for health, that higher intake helps preserve lean mass when energy is deficient, and that some sources, especially animal-based ones, offer higher-quality protein. 

Questions such as optimal intake per meal, timing, and the long-term effects of very  high-protein diets remain far less settled than popular discourse  suggests.

The honest answer is less exciting than the headline  promises. Protein deserves its place on the plate, just not on the  pedestal we’ve built for it. Protein matters, especially for preserving  muscle during aging or weight loss, but it isn't a stand-alone marker of  a healthy diet.

Jesus tells us how he intends to be visibly glorified in the world: in his people. “The glory that you have given me I have given to them… I in them” (John 17:22–23).

Catholics and Orthodox are proposing something completely foreign to the pages of Scripture: that devotion offered to a man-made image passes through the image to Christ, and through Christ to the Father???

But Jesus actually tells us where our love for something visible passes on to him:

“As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.” (Matt. 25:40)

If you want to show your love and devotion to Christ through something visible, show love to real, living, breathing people here and now. Feed the hungry. Clothe the naked. Visit the sick. Love your brothers and sisters.

That is the principle Christ actually gives us. Not “what you do to an image of me, you do to me,” but “what you do to them, you do to me.”

The Church is Christ’s body, being conformed to his image and making him visible to the world through our love for one another (John 13:35; Rom. 8:29; 1 Cor. 12:27; 2 Cor. 3:18).

I don’t need to manufacture an image of Christ. Christ is making his image out of us.

text:
$BGDE This will be a long post. For that I do apologize. Today is the 115th day of leading the charge for Big Digital Energy. To sum it up, it has been an experience. Perhaps the most fun I have had in business, and I've had my fair share. I get asked all the time: who are you, where did you come from, what's your experience in this industry, and where are you really taking this company? I think it's time to share some of my personal story with you. For those of you who have invested your hard-earned dollars with us, and to those who are considering it, I owe you that much.

My name is Joshua Kilgore, and today is my 45th birthday. Born in Tennessee, I grew up in the Mid-West, living in TN, IL, OH, and KY before I ultimately landed in Wayzata, MN at the age of 11. I grew up in a traditional middle-class family with parents who loved me (still do, I'm told 🤣) and two younger sisters. Like a lot of children, I lived in a bubble. Carefree, with no worries other than the anticipation of my next soccer game and learning how to play hockey with kids who started on ice skates at birth. That ended shortly. The summer I turned 12, my parents informed us they were divorcing…bubble burst. Life was going to change in a major way. Two households to pay for, attorneys working hard for those billable hours, and family infighting that I didn't know could exist started to set the tone for what the next decade would bring. A year later, my father made the decision to move to Arkansas, where he and my mother were from, for a fresh start. I had the opportunity multiple times to join him, but I was torn between moving and leaving my mother and two younger sisters 800 miles north, so I stayed. I don't regret that decision because while there were hardships, there were good times, good friends, and opportunities which presented that I learned to take control of.

In high school I was introduced to a corporate attorney in the area who recruited hockey players for Amherst College, his alma mater, when he wasn't putting deals together. I was no academic, and by that time the only hockey I played was pick-up games, but I had impressed him with my demeanor and work ethic. He hired me to work at his estate and then recommended me to work for the Carlson family on their estate, where the star hockey recruits would typically be given summer jobs between semesters. The Carlson Estate was another world to me. I had never seen homes so grand, personal fleets of boats, or Ferraris up close. Literally up close, as one of my duties was to keep them all detailed. The opportunity and experience opened my mind and created a drive in me that didn't previously exist. I didn't want to be poor anymore. I didn't want to buy secondhand clothes or have to worry about putting gas in the tank. Curt Carlson founded the Gold Bond Stamp Company and turned that endeavor into the Carlson Companies. He started from nothing and built a multi-billion-dollar empire that he passed to his children. Anything was now possible. I needed to figure out a way to create something for myself.

A few years later, during my time at the University of Minnesota, I went to Arkansas to visit my father. He and my uncle encouraged me to transfer to the University of Arkansas and join them in skilled nursing, which was their business. It was an industry I never wanted to be a part of, but the idea that I could work my way into ownership sealed the deal, and I committed. In January 2003, I made the move with my fiancée (now my wife) and took the plunge.

Unfortunately, six months after I made the move, my father and uncle's relationship hit a wall and they decided to part ways. The deal I had agreed to changed overnight, and I was out of a job. My father was able to secure a single location out of the deal, but it wasn't big enough for the two of us to live comfortably, so we set a path to work towards expanding operations. After some time we were able to secure a second location, which then turned into a third, fourth, and fifth. I began to experiment with business outside of our partnership and added two locations of my own in a new state, as well as an interest in a group that provided dental services to skilled patients who otherwise were not able to receive them. My place as an entrepreneur was sealed. With that came some real tests.

Skilled nursing is a very intense industry where a hundred things can go wrong even while you're doing everything right. I also learned what having partners that don't have the same level of commitment and ethics can do to an operation. I walked away from the dental services company because I caught my partner being unethical in another branch of the company, only to get sued by him after moving to another partnership and starting over. It was a trying experience, but I came out victorious and learned invaluable lessons from that ordeal about how to fight, how to defend, and why it's so important to always do the right thing, even when it's not the easy thing. ExcelHealth Group was born from that experience and today is one of the largest providers in our industry. My partner, our CEO, has been instrumental in both building our team and making sure we always show up and do the right thing. Again, even when it's not easy. The payoff from doing the right thing? ExcelHealth has the opportunity to be a billion-dollar market cap company in the years ahead. Continuing to execute will be paramount.

By 2015, I had created a large enough position and was able to buy my father out and let him enjoy retirement. I rebranded, rebuilt, and set my eyes on forward growth. In 2018, after having several peers in the industry approach me about a buyout, I decided to lease out all of my properties and focus on building a true portfolio, REIT style. In 2020, when COVID was taking over the world and crushing our industry, I made my first move in the State of Texas, buying my first location and backing two young operators who had the work ethic and discipline I could put real money behind. That started a snowball effect, and over the next four years I put together a number of large transactions that brought my ownership to 27 locations across three states with a strong diversity of operating tenants. The value of what we put together was so great that in the summer of 2025 I started getting offers for the portfolio. The money was there, the time was right, and I had other interests that I thought I could leverage into that would continue to accelerate. All in, over $400M worth of deals I had put together were sold in three tranches, and that allowed me to take the plunge into powered land assets.

I had been participating in the Bitcoin mining space with my partners Phil Stanley and Cody Smith since 2021 with one-off projects, but as we each had liquidity events to deal with and a tax burden to solve for, we decided to form an official partnership and created Big Digital Energy, LLC (now renamed Six Thirty AI, LLC since we gave our fun name to the pubco) in the summer of 2025. The thesis was simple. We believed powered land was undervalued, Bitcoin mining misunderstood and underappreciated, and that pulling together both our expertise and liquidity would allow us to quickly build a portfolio we could further build on with the AI race squarely in front of us. In less than six months we put together a collection of sites that many PubCos in the space today still can't compete with.

Phil, Cody, and I have always been equities and options guys. I have been trading for over 20 years. In November 2025, when Mawson announced their 20:1 reverse split, the stock tanked and stood out on my watch list. I ran some quick numbers and discovered the company was trading for less than $100K per MW they controlled, at the same time we were developing locations for $300-500K per megawatt. It was a value buy, and I was in. I rang Phil and Cody and pitched it to them. They didn't disagree. Over the next few days, as the stock continued to fall, I continued to buy. At some point along the way, Cody reached out and said, "Josh, I think you might have to file your position with the SEC." Having been in private business for as long as I had, I was honestly not aware of the thresholds because it was never a factor in my other investing.

At that time, we decided to reach out to the company as substantial shareholders because they were obviously struggling to maintain the business and we were quite good at it. Over the course of the following three weeks, we tried every way we could think of to touch base with executive leadership, the Board, employees, etc., and they simply refused to talk to us. If we are anything, we are "Persistent," and finally, after dozens of emails, DMs, texts, etc., Mawson agreed to have a call with us on Christmas Eve morning.

The first conversation included GC Kaliste Saloom and CFO Bill Regan, as well as one of their outside advisors. It went great, and those communications continued through the holidays. Noticeably absent was the Board, as they still refused to entertain a call, which led to Kaliste calling me on January 7th ahead of their next Board meeting, which was the following day. Kaliste asked if we could put our ideas to help the company in black and white so he could present them to the Board in an effort to get them to open up to a conversation. At his request, we put together a bullet-point list of ideas. The document was labeled a draft, for discussion purposes only, and contained a number of bullet points summarizing different ideas we had discussed about how to work with them and possibly fund them out of some of the issues. We felt pretty good about it, but Mawson went silent and never responded. A couple of weeks later, a lawsuit arrived alleging we failed to file with the SEC correctly, that we didn't disclose our true intent to take them over (false), that we should not have been allowed to buy the shares we had, AND that we had made an offer for the Company that we did not disclose to the market (also false). We were admittedly blown away by the allegations considering the quality of the conversations we had with Kaliste, but now understood what we were really dealing with. A Board so focused on litigation they couldn't do good business if it was brought to them on a silver platter. Twenty years of litigation experience and a recent win against two attorneys general gave me the mental fortitude and confidence that this was not something to be afraid of. We needed to prove them wrong and usher them out.

After two months of litigation, we won on a Motion for Summary Judgment. Mawson had no claim, no case. They had crossed the line, and it was time to remove them from an industry they really didn't belong in. During the suit, we had investors from around the world reach out to us in support of our actions, encouraging us to make a move and fix this company. We hired Olshan to represent us in a proxy fight to remove the Board. As we were gearing up to collect shareholder votes via the proxy solicitation process, the Board finally wised up and decided to walk away and save face. They agreed to vote Phil and Cody, as well as three independents, onto the new Board, but refused to vote me on out of spite. I was made aware of this just days before this transition was to take place. I laughed it off and let them have their emotional win, knowing the trust I had in my partners. As a parting gift, the market told the former board what it really thought about their leadership and sold the stock down to $1.70 on their last trading day at the helm, Friday, April 3, 2026. We took control the following Monday, April 6th, and never looked back. That is the true story of how we actually got here.

Fast forward: we have now been at the helm for 115 days. In my personal view, our team has accomplished so much, and always with the best interests of the Company and Shareholders in mind. I think very few people can really understand and appreciate the task we took on and what we have given up for the good of the Company, noting, of course, that as the largest shareholders we have the most to win and lose from our decisions.

To those of you still reading, I want to say thank you. Thank you for your time, your trust, and your confidence in this team. I am not a one-man show. I could not do this without the incredible people around me. That has been true in all of my endeavors. My goal is to always be the dumbest guy in the room, and to date, I have always hit that goal.

My name is Joshua Kilgore. I am 45. I am a Son, a Husband, and a Father to two amazing children and one black lab (she's adopted but we don't tell her 😉). I'm also a Serial Entrepreneur.

I am the Executive Chairman of Big Digital Energy, Inc.

I am a proud partner in Six Thirty AI, LLC.

I am the Founder and Principal of Endeavor Blockchain, LLC.

I am a seed investor and Board member of Corley Energy, LLC.

I am Founder and Principal of Kilgore Property Management, LLC.

I am Co-Founder and Managing Partner of ExcelHealth Group, LLC.

There is so much more ahead. I look forward to experiencing the journey with you all. Thank you again for your continued support. We will not let you down. Big Digital Energy things ahead!

text:
Time to dust off the Civil War history chops. Here’s the story of the worst maritime disaster in US history, that almost nobody knows about. 

It’s April 1865. Lee surrendered to Grant on the 9th, and the remaining rebel armies will surrender over the coming weeks. As hostilities wind down, Union POWs are pouring out of Confederate prison camps like Andersonville and Cahaba. These men are barefoot, starved, sick, and vermin-ridden. All over the south, these straggling masses of humanity gather in makeshift camps without proper tents or blankets, hoping for transport home. 

To help solve this humanitarian crisis, the federal government offers steamboat companies on the Mississippi River around $2.75 per enlisted man and $8.00 per officer to ferry them north. The average ticket for deck passage from Vicksburg, Mississippi to Cairo, Illinois was around $5. Inflation was rampant during this time. So steamboat operators were incentivized to load as many people as possible, as quickly and cheaply as possible.

On April 23rd, the steamboat Sultana docked at Vicksburg to deal with a leaking boiler. An engineer recommended a major repair, but the captain ordered a quick patch instead. He was unwilling to risk losing a valuable government contract, and even greased the palms of the local Army quartermaster to ensure Sultana got a full load. 

The boat was legally rated for 376 passengers. She left Vicksburg and headed north with over 2,500 aboard. 

At 2am on the 27th, near Memphis, the patched boiler exploded. An estimated 400 people were killed instantly, and Sultana quickly became an inferno. The remaining passengers and crew went into the river, which was freezing and flooded from the spring runoff. Most of the former POWs were too weak to swim and either drowned or succumbed to hypothermia. 

At least 1,547 people died, and many estimates run upwards of 1,800. For reference, the Titanic killed 1,512. 

It remains the worst maritime disaster in American history, yet almost nobody has heard of it. 

Even at the time, the story was buried by another news item: president Lincoln’s assassination. He was shot on April 14th, and the perpetrator John Wilkes Booth had been cornered and killed just a day before the Sultana exploded, on the 26th. Every front page in the country was running that story. If the Sultana was mentioned in northern newspapers, it was typically in the form of a short notice. Harper’s Weekly covered it. That was about it. 

The ship’s captain died in the disaster, and only one other officer (an Army captain who oversaw the loading of newly released prisoners onto transports) was charged. His court-martial dragged on for months, partly because key witnesses (like the corrupt quartermaster I mentioned) hastily resigned their commissions and thus, as civilians, could ignore a military subpoena. 

Eventually the captain was convicted and sentenced to dismissal, but this was overturned. The Army’s judge advocate general ruled that while the boat had been overcrowded, it was not overLOADED….. and the boiler explosion had nothing to do with the weight of the passengers. No one else was ever held accountable.

A bit of additional trivia: pic related is a photograph of the overloaded Sultana taken at a stop in Arkansas, the day before she exploded. As the men gathered to one side to be in the shot, the boat began to list. Right after this photo was taken, they were ordered back before it went over.

As an acquaintance of Campe's, that old usurer, parjure and maid-wife-widower, you must have been aware that this individual is one of my mortal enemies, and hence you had no right to offer him my pamphlet,b thereby affording him the opportunity he desired of conveying his impertinences to me indirectly and at no risk to himself. EXCLUSIVE: Watchdog Sounds Alarm On The Left’s Massive Foreign Money Pipeline | Francis Kapper, Daily Caller News Foundation

A government watchdog group is urging lawmakers to crack down on foreign money flowing into U.S. nonprofits that influence American politics and public policy, according to letters exclusively obtained by the Daily Caller News Foundation.

Americans for Public Trust (APT) is sending letters to all 50 governors and officials on six congressional committees directing them to its newly launched https://t.co/giOyrPyYyK database, which has cataloged a running total of more than $5 billion flowing from foreign governments, foreign nationals and foreign charities into U.S.-based nonprofits with records dating back to 2002. The group is calling on state and federal officials to examine whether existing laws adequately prevent foreign actors from indirectly influencing political outcomes.

“The information is available. The threat is real,” APT Executive Director Caitlin Sutherland wrote in the letters.

Federal law broadly prohibits foreign nationals from making contributions, donations, expenditures and disbursements in connection with U.S. elections, but foreign money can still finance certain activities through tax-exempt organizations, advocacy groups, voter registration efforts and other channels, according to APT.

The Senate could next take up the Stop Foreign Funds in Elections Act after the House approved the legislation in July. The bill would extend the federal prohibition on foreign-national contributions and donations to ballot initiatives and referenda.

Federal lobbying disclosures show Common Cause, a nonpartisan government watchdog and democracy advocacy organization, and union powerhouse AFL-CIO have lobbied on the Stop Foreign Funds in Elections Act, though the filings do not indicate whether the organizations supported or opposed the legislation. The groups didn’t respond to a request for comment.

The foreign money comes from a collection of overseas foundations and foreign-linked philanthropic networks. An earlier APT analysis identified six major sources that it said had collectively directed more than $2.65 billion into U.S. advocacy groups.

Hansjörg Wyss is a Swiss billionaire who uses his massive wealth to fund liberal and progressive advocacy groups in the United States. Nonprofits associated with Wyss accounted for approximately $673 million, according to APT.

His Wyss Foundation, a private charitable foundation, and Berger Action Fund, a nonprofit advocacy group, have directed more than $372 million into nonprofits associated with the Arabella Advisors network, a group of major liberal nonprofit funding vehicles, including nearly $305 million from Berger Action Fund to the Sixteen Thirty Fund, a liberal nonprofit dark money group, according to APT’s database.

“Americans for Public Trust is a right-wing organization bought and paid for by Leonard Leo that has repeatedly targeted Sixteen Thirty Fund because of our support for progressive causes,” a Sixteen Thirty spokesperson told the DCNF. “If the group were genuinely concerned about our campaign finance system, it would join us in supporting meaningful reforms that would increase transparency rather than selectively attacking organizations it ideologically opposes. We are proud of our work and operate in full compliance with the laws and regulations governing 501(c)(4) organizations. We strictly follow legal requirements regarding use of foreign funding.”

The Wyss Foundation and Berger Action Fund did not respond to a request for comment.

Other climate activist groups, like British billionaire Christopher Hohn’s Children’s Investment Fund Foundation, accounted for about $638.2 million, according to APT. The Children’s Investment Fund Foundation did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

APT’s materials identify several major climate and environmental organizations among the largest recipients of foreign funding. The database lists the ClimateWorks Foundation, a U.S.-based public charity that connects philanthropic funders with climate change initiatives around the world, as receiving $582 million, according to the database.

ClimateWorks has distributed more than $2 billion to over 850 grantees in 50 countries since 2008, its website says. The organization did not respond to a request for comment.

APT’s database also lists Energy Foundation China at $104 million from the U.K.-based Children’s Investment Fund Foundation and Quadrature Climate Foundation, and the Swiss-based Oak Foundation. The California-registered grantmaking charity has operated in China since 1999 and says it supports research, policy development and international cooperation aimed at transforming China’s energy sector and achieving greenhouse gas emissions neutrality.

Energy Foundation China did not respond to a request for comment.

The money has flowed into a mix of political advocacy groups and major environmental organizations.

The Sixteen Thirty Fund, a nonprofit advocacy organization that backs left-wing causes ranging from voting access and health care to climate policy and racial equity, received $305 million from the Berger Action Fund, according to APT’s database.

The group also fiscally sponsors Chorus, a program that reportedly contacted dozens of Democratic-aligned social media influencers in June 2025 and offered participants up to $8,000 per month to promote left-wing messaging online. House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer launched an investigation into the program on Nov. 19, 2025, seeking records on its contracts, funding and compliance practices amid concerns about the secrecy surrounding the payments.

The Berger Action Fund gave another $102 million to Fund for a Better Future, a social-welfare nonprofit that funds and fiscally sponsors projects involving elections, immigration, climate policy and other left-wing causes, according to the database.

The fund has also bankrolled Democratic-aligned advocacy, giving nearly $5.1 million to Building Back Together, which was founded by former Biden campaign staffers to promote the Biden administration’s agenda, between 2021 and 2023, according to InfluenceWatch. It also gave $1 million to Planned Parenthood Action Fund, Planned Parenthood’s political and lobbying arm, in 2017, InfluenceWatch data shows.

Fund for a Better Future did not respond to a request for comment.

The funding also extended deep into the environmental advocacy world. APT lists the Environmental Defense Fund, a global environmental nonprofit that uses scientific research, economic analysis, advocacy and litigation to advance climate and energy policies, as receiving a total of $48 million from multiple donors. The Environmental Defense Fund did not respond to a request for comment.

The Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), which employs lawyers, scientists and policy specialists to advocate and litigate on climate, energy, wildlife and public-health issues, received another $30 million, according to the database.

“NRDC is a U.S-based public interest organization that advocates for clean, American-made energy that can power the nation and address the climate crisis,” NRDC spokesperson Mark Drajem told the DCNF. “Our priorities and positions are set by our professional staff and our independent, U.S.-based board of trustees, and no one else. The funds highlighted in this database went to helping reduce pollution and protect wildlife in countries outside the United States.”

Some of those funding streams can be traced back to major overseas climate philanthropies.

Quadrature Climate Foundation, created by the founders of London-based hedge fund Quadrature Capital, has directed more than $568 million to U.S.-based organizations, according to the database. ClimateWorks alone received $148 million from Quadrature, including grants that APT says were designated for efforts to accelerate electric-vehicle adoption and push financial regulators to address climate-related risks. Quadrature Capital did not respond to a request for comment.

At the state level, APT pointed to Nebraska, Iowa, Missouri and Ohio as states that have taken steps targeting foreign funding in ballot measure campaigns.

The congressional letter was addressed to the leadership of the House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform and Ways and Means committees; along with the Senate Judiciary, Rules and Administration and Finance committees.

Is full-term abortion enough to get Evangelicals to the polls?

Nine states and the District of Columbia still have no time limit. In those places a child can be legally killed at eight months—with a heartbeat, a face, and a real chance of living outside the womb. After Dobbs, the national number did not crash. There are still more than a million abortions a year.

That is the country Evangelicals keep calling a “Christian decline” while most of them do not bother to vote.

Steve Deace has spent years laying out the cost: if this bloc had voted in force in the elections already lost, the country would not be this close to coming apart. That is not hype. It is the turnout record he has cited. The upcoming midterms are the next chance to stop treating that record as someone else’s problem.

In 2012, roughly 2.5 million fewer Evangelicals voted than in 2008.
That drop helped decide battleground states even as independents moved the other way.
At least six million Evangelicals still voted to re-elect Barack Obama.
In 2014, when they did turn out, Republicans got more Evangelical votes than Democrats got from every non-white voter combined, and Senate seats in the South followed.
The pattern has not changed.
When white Evangelicals fall below about 25 percent of the electorate, or when a candidate only gets the 76 percent share of 2020 instead of the 80 percent share of 2016, the other side wins.
In 2024 they were 22 percent of the electorate—the lowest Trump-era share, matching 2012—even though 81 percent of those who voted still backed him.
Iowa showed the same warning Deace pointed out: Evangelicals fell from 64 percent of caucus-goers in 2016 to 55 percent.

George Barna’s research before that cycle made the size of the problem plain: tens of millions of born-again adults, including tens of millions who go to church with some regularity, were ready to sit it out. Not interested in politics. Did not like the candidates. Figured one vote would not matter. Then the same churches spend the next two years complaining about the schools, the border, what is being taught to kids, and how empty the pews are getting. That is not persecution. That is staying home and then acting shocked.

Deace has also named what is coming next. Heretics are failing in the pulpit. When they take over churches and denominations, attendance collapses. So they are running for office and using campaigns as a bigger stage for that heresy than the churches they wrecked could ever give them. That is Rob Sand in Iowa and James Talarico in Texas. Deace says they are not exceptions. They are a warning. This will be the next wave of Democrat candidates for years to come: a party that went from “my faith does not shape my politics” to “my politics is the stage for my false faith.” Campaigns are going to look like rival revival meetings. People are hungry again for deeper truth and guidance. If they are not offered the real thing, they will take the fake version over a polished official who offers no meaning at all. If the Right does not run candidates who can speak to that, it will lose elections in places that used to be safe.

Deace has called white Evangelicals the last line of defense against the spirit of the age. The voting math backs him up. A group cannot say America is losing its Christian inheritance and then treat voting as optional while the other side turns elections into a pulpit. A country is not held together by feel-good sermons. It is held together by majorities. Some of the most-churched states in America have spent a generation picking the weakest Republicans their open primaries will give them, then acting surprised when the culture keeps moving left. Showing up on Sunday is not the same thing as showing up when it counts. Salt that stays in the shaker does not save anything.

Become warriors for God in the places He actually gave—the family, the church, and the vote—or quit complaining about the country’s morals decline.

Vote!
